blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: Balance sheet: working capital, and the three ratios that reveal stress / OAS: eligibility, the clawback threshold, and deferral math / Explaining risk: expected outcomes, ranges, and the language of probability
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Statement forensics, lesson 3: Balance sheet: working capital, and the three ratios that reveal stress.

Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities. It tells you whether a company can fund its own operations without borrowing more or selling something it needs. When it shrinks fast, that is usually the first place stress shows up, before it ever hits the income statement.

Three ratios do the real work here. First, the current ratio: current assets divided by current liabilities. Second, the quick ratio: same thing, but you strip out inventory, because inventory is the slowest asset to turn into cash. Third, the cash conversion cycle: days inventory outstanding plus days sales outstanding, minus days payable outstanding. That third one tells you how long cash is tied up before it comes back to the company.

Take a mid-cap industrial distributor. Current assets: 1.4 billion dollars. Current liabilities: 900 million. Current ratio is 1.56. Looks fine. Now strip inventory, which is 600 million of those current assets. Quick ratio drops to 0.89. That is below 1, meaning without selling inventory, the company cannot cover what it owes in the next twelve months. Then check the cash conversion cycle: 58 days inventory, 45 days receivables, 30 days payables. That is 73 days of cash tied up before it returns. If that number was 55 days two years ago, that is the story. In Thomson ONE, you get all three inputs off the balance sheet tab under Financials, and the DSO, DIO, DPO figures usually sit in the ratios or financial analysis section.

The mistake people make is reading the current ratio alone and calling it healthy. A current ratio above 1 hides a lot if inventory is bloated or slow moving. You need the quick ratio to see past that, and you need the cycle to see the trend, not just the snapshot.

Your task today: pull the last two fiscal years of balance sheet data for one company you know well, in Thomson ONE, and calculate all three ratios for both years. Fifteen minutes, no more. You are looking for direction, not a single number.

This tells you liquidity risk. It does not tell you profitability, and it does not tell you why cash is tied up. That comes next, with the cash flow statement.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 9: OAS: eligibility, the clawback threshold, and deferral math.

The single biggest OAS surprise for incorporated business owners is this: the clawback is based on taxable income, not cash income, and dividends get grossed up before that test applies. A business owner paying themselves eligible dividends can look modest on a bank statement and still get hammered on line 23600 of the tax return.

Here is how Old Age Security actually works. You qualify at 65 if you have lived in Canada at least 10 years after age 18. Full pension needs 40 years of residency after 18. Fewer years gives you a partial pension, one fortieth of the full amount per year of residency. For 2026, the maximum OAS payment at 65 is roughly 735 dollars a month, about 8,820 dollars a year, and it is indexed quarterly to inflation.

Now the clawback, officially the OAS Recovery Tax. For 2026, the threshold is approximately 95,800 dollars of net income. Above that line, you repay 15 cents of OAS for every dollar of income over the threshold, up to a full clawback around 155,000 dollars for someone 65 to 74.

Worked example. Client has net income of 130,000 dollars in 2026. That is 34,200 dollars over the 95,800 threshold. Multiply by 15 percent: 5,130 dollars gets clawed back over the following payment year. Against 8,820 dollars of annual OAS, that is 58 percent gone.

Deferral math is clean. Delay past 65 and OAS grows 0.6 percent per month, up to 60 months at age 70, for a maximum 36 percent increase. That turns 735 dollars into just over 1,000 dollars a month for life, and if income is high at 65 and drops later, deferral also sidesteps years of clawback.

The mistake: assuming OAS clawback tracks cash flow. It does not. Eligible dividends are grossed up by 38 percent before they hit net income, so a business owner drawing dividends can trigger clawback at a much lower real cash number than a T4 employee would.

Communication, lesson 9: Explaining risk: expected outcomes, ranges, and the language of probability.

In 1951, a CIA analyst named Sherman Kent wrote that a Soviet attack on Yugoslavia was a "serious possibility." Policymakers read that phrase and argued for weeks about what it meant. So Kent later surveyed his own colleagues and asked them to attach a number to "serious possibility." The answers ranged from 20 percent to 80 percent. Same words, wildly different meanings. That is the entire problem with explaining risk in language instead of numbers.

When you explain risk to a client, give three things every time: the expected outcome, the range around it, and a stated probability. Not adjectives. Numbers.

Here is a worked example. Say a client asks whether their portfolio will grow. Per S&P Dow Jones Indices, the S&P 500 has averaged roughly 10 percent a year since 1950. That is your expected outcome. But in any single year, returns have ranged from a loss of 37 percent in 2008 to a gain of 32 percent in 2013. That is your range. And historically, about one year in four has ended negative. That is your probability. So the honest sentence is: expect around 8 to 10 percent a year on average, but in any given year it could swing from a 20 percent loss to a 30 percent gain, and there is roughly a one in four chance it is a down year.

The mistake people make is collapsing all three into one confident number. "This will grow 8 percent." That is false precision. It sounds authoritative in the meeting and then it breaks trust the first year reality misses it, which undoes everything you built in the bad-news lesson.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: Pull two fiscal years of balance sheet data for one company in Thomson ONE and calculate the current ratio, quick ratio, and cash conversion cycle for both years, noting the direction of change.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull one client's line 23600 from their most recent notice of assessment, compare it to the 95,800 dollar 2026 threshold, and note whether dividend gross-up is inflating that number relative to their actual cash income.
Communication: Take one outcome you regularly discuss with clients or board members, and write it as three sentences: expected value, range, and probability, each with a real number attached.

blocks.label: Markets & Economy
blocks.title: Markets Rally on AI Optimism, Oil Eases
blocks.script:
Good morning. Global markets started the week higher, lifted by a rally in technology stocks and a pullback in oil prices, as investors looked ahead to this week's summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

According to The Globe and Mail's Before the Bell newsletter, the pan-European STOXX 600 rose about one percent, with Britain's FTSE, Germany's DAX and France's CAC all posting gains. Hong Kong's Hang Seng also climbed, while Japanese markets were closed for a holiday.

On Bay Street the mood was more mixed. The TSX slipped about 0.2 percent, while on Wall Street the S&P 500 and Nasdaq edged higher and the Dow dipped slightly, according to a market snapshot from The Peak. The Canadian dollar traded near 71.5 US cents.

Oil prices retreated from highs seen last week above 109 US dollars a barrel, with Brent and West Texas Intermediate both falling more than 2 percent on hopes of diplomatic progress on the Iran conflict, including a possible Trump meeting with Iran's president on the sidelines of this week's UN General Assembly, Bloomberg reported.

Bloomberg's Markets Daily newsletter also flagged growing unease about how much of the market's gains now rest on artificial intelligence. It noted AI-related spending accounts for roughly half of recent US GDP growth, and that nearly 33 trillion dollars has been added to S&P 500 valuations since late 2022, mostly tied to AI-linked companies. Fund managers told Bloomberg that diversifying away from that exposure has become difficult given how deeply AI is now woven through markets.

Feeding that boom, SoftBank is reportedly seeking to raise more than 11 billion dollars in what would be one of the largest junk bond deals ever, to help fund its investments in OpenAI.

Bloomberg also detailed a market meltdown in Turkey, where regulators cracked down on asset managers accused of artificially inflating illiquid stocks. Executives, including the chairman of asset manager Tera, have been arrested, and a finance company chairman's fortune, once valued near 14 billion dollars, is reportedly evaporating as authorities liquidate seized funds at steep discounts.

In corporate news, chipmaker AMD joined the trillion-dollar club, following Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron, on continued AI-driven demand, the Globe and Mail reported.

Paramount Skydance and California officials made progress in settlement talks over its 110 billion dollar acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, with terms reportedly including a commitment to release 30 films a year in theatres, the BBC reported.

And in Canadian wealth management, Richardson Wealth announced it will rebrand as Nobelia Wealth this November, following its acquisition by iA Financial last year.

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem was scheduled to speak in Halifax today, with markets also watching Canada's July construction investment data.
talkingPoints: Global stocks rose on AI-led optimism and cooling oil prices ahead of the Trump-Xi summit.
Oil pulled back on hopes of Iran diplomacy, though analysts warn the broader trend remains upward.
Bloomberg warns AI now underpins roughly half of US GDP growth and trillions in stock market gains, raising concentration risk.
SoftBank plans an over 11 billion dollar junk bond sale to fund further OpenAI investment.
Turkish regulators are unwinding funds accused of inflating illiquid stocks, wiping out fortunes.
AMD becomes the fourth US chipmaker to reach a trillion-dollar valuation.
Paramount and California near a settlement clearing its Warner Bros Discovery merger.
Richardson Wealth will become Nobelia Wealth in November under owner iA Financial.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: BlackBerry, Irving Oil, PSP Lead Canadian Business News
blocks.script:
BlackBerry is the story getting the most airtime in Canadian business circles right now. The Waterloo firm has rebuilt itself around embedded software for cars through its QNX platform, and the Globe and Mail reports it just secured a deal worth more than $100 million for a new automotive software product called Alloy Kore, landing before the product's official release later this year. The tailwind is obvious: a nine figure contract ahead of launch validates years of pivoting away from handsets and toward the car. The headwind is concentration risk, this is one customer, one product line, and the auto software space has deep pocketed rivals circling the same real estate inside every vehicle's dashboard. An evidence-based advisor would tell you a single contract headline is not a valuation, and that chasing the stock on the news release is speculation dressed up as analysis.

Irving Oil is next. The privately held Saint John refiner, one of the largest fuel suppliers in Atlantic Canada, has named Austrian energy executive Alfred Stern as its next chief executive, taking over November first from Jeff Matthews, who is retiring, the Globe reports, after a strategic review. The tailwind is a fresh, internationally seasoned hand brought in specifically after that review, suggesting the family ownership wants growth beyond the East Coast refinery footprint. The headwind is the review itself: when a private company brings in outside leadership after months of soul-searching, it usually means change is coming, and change at a company this size ripples through Atlantic Canada's fuel supply and jobs. An evidence-based advisor would simply note Irving Oil is private, so there is no ticker to buy, only indirect energy sector exposure through diversified funds.

Third is a story about airports, but really about who runs them. Montreal-based PSP Investments, the pension manager for federal public servants, already owns airports abroad through its AviAlliance subsidiary, and Globe commentary this week names it as the natural anchor for a global champion in a critical infrastructure sector once Ottawa sells concessions at Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto and Montreal. The tailwind is scale and existing expertise, PSP already runs terminals overseas. The headwind is competition, other Canadian pension giants and foreign operators want the same concessions, and the politics of selling off national infrastructure are touchy. An evidence-based advisor would point out you likely already own a slice of this story through your own pension exposure, so there is nothing new to chase here.

StubHub is fourth. The ticket resale platform got hit with a $20,000 fine from Ontario, the Globe reports, under the province's new law capping resale prices, though the provincial website does not specify what events the penalties were linked to. The tailwind, if there is one, is that compliance signals the secondary ticket market is being taken seriously by regulators rather than ignored. The headwind is that this fine could be the first of many across provinces now watching resale pricing closely, and repeated penalties chip away at a platform's margins and reputation. An evidence-based advisor would say a $20,000 fine is immaterial to a company of StubHub's size, and headline regulatory risk should not drive a portfolio decision either way.

Fifth, a private rail bet on the Rockies. Liricon Capital and Plenary Americas have filed a passenger-rail proposal with the Alberta government for a Calgary-to-Banff line, the Globe reports, with the consortium saying it could be running by 2030. The tailwind is obvious tourist demand and a government that has been receptive to nation-building infrastructure pitches. The headwind is that Alberta has seen ambitious rail plans stall before, and financing, environmental review, and municipal buy-in all still need to fall into place. An evidence-based advisor would note this is a private consortium deal, not something retail investors can buy into directly, so treat it as a story to watch rather than a trade.

Sixth is Vero, an artificial intelligence tool built to lower legal costs for small business owners. The Globe reports critics say the technology is still young and isn't close to being able to replicate much of the work that lawyers do. The tailwind is real demand from small businesses priced out of legal advice. The headwind is liability, if the tool gets something wrong on a contract or a dispute, who is on the hook, and regulators overseeing legal practice are watching closely. An evidence-based advisor would call this an interesting signal of where professional services are heading, not an investable idea today, since it is a private venture with no public shares.

Last, the cannabis sector, led by names like High Tide, Canopy Growth and Aurora Cannabis. The Globe reports the industry is warning Ottawa that Canada could lose its lead in global cannabis exports without federal backing, with the sector forecasting two billion dollars in foreign sales by 2027. The tailwind is Canada's early regulatory head start and moves like High Tide's expansion into the German medical market. The headwind is the total absence of a federal export strategy, leaving producers to build international beachheads alone while global competitors catch up fast. An evidence-based advisor would remind a client these remain small, volatile stocks, sized as a speculative sliver of a portfolio, never a core holding.

None of tonight's watch list names, the Bank of Canada rate decision, Dimensional Fund Advisors, Scotia Wealth Management, Manitoba Hydro, United Way Winnipeg, the Jets or the Bombers, turned up in the business and markets coverage driving this block over the past 48 hours.

Irving Oil is bringing in an Austrian energy executive as CEO after a strategic review.
Ottawa's airport privatization plan could hand a Canadian pension fund a global infrastructure business.
StubHub just got fined by Ontario under the province's new ticket resale price cap.
Cannabis companies say Canada could lose its export lead without federal support.

blocks.script:
Oil is back above one hundred US dollars a barrel, and that is now the biggest variable in your rate outlook for the next year. Wealth Professional reports that shipping disruptions tied to the Strait of Hormuz have driven crude above that mark and are pushing the US Federal Reserve's rate cut window out into 2027. Brent eased back toward 101 dollars on Monday as traders hoped for a diplomatic breakthrough on Iran ahead of this week's United Nations meeting, but the ten year US Treasury yield was still hovering near five per cent after breaking through that level on Friday. Higher for longer in Washington makes it harder for the Bank of Canada to cut further here, even with a softer domestic economy.

That is your live watch item today. Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem is speaking in Halifax this morning, his first public remarks since the Bank held its overnight rate at 2.25% earlier this month. MoneySense is asking outright whether a hike, not a cut, could be coming in October, given renewed inflation pressure from oil and a softer loonie, which traded near 71.4 US cents on Monday. If you have clients renewing variable rate mortgages or leveraged investment loans this fall, this is the one to flag before the "why did my payment go up" call comes in.

Two other Wealth Professional pieces belong in the same conversation. Nearly half of working Canadians now describe themselves as financially stressed, and new research pegs the resulting hit to employer productivity at 74.3 billion dollars a year. Separately, a Deloitte Canada report finds health related barriers to workforce participation cost the country more than 100 billion dollars in economic output in 2025. Financial stress and health issues feed each other. If a client mentions they have been off work or running on empty, that is not small talk, that is a trigger to review disability coverage and check whether their plan still matches their capacity to earn.

On home turf, here is what to know for any Manitoba client who raises their tax bill this fall. Manitoba's 2026 budget, tabled by Finance Minister Adrien Sala in March, held the line on rates. No changes are proposed to the corporate income tax rates or the CA$500,000 small-business limit. But CBC reports the province has stopped indexing its own personal tax brackets to inflation this year, and the Canadian Taxpayers Federation says that bracket creep will cost Manitoba filers 82 million dollars next year. Provincial sales tax also starts applying to software subscriptions and data storage as of January 1. On the credit side, for the 2027 property tax year, Manitoba will increase the Homeowners Affordability Tax Credit by $100, from $1,600 to $1,700, and for the 2027 tax year, the Renters Affordability Tax Credit will increase to $675, while the seniors' top-up will rise to a maximum of $385.71 for individuals with a family net income below $40,000. Nothing here moves your model, but it is useful small talk for the fall review meeting.

Now the one that actually changes advice. If you have incorporated physician or professional clients sitting on retained earnings inside a corporation, remind them that this year's small business deduction depends on last year's passive income, not this year's. A CCPC calculating its 2026 SBD uses the passive income earned in its 2025 taxation year, so investment returns earned in 2026 will affect the tax rate on active income next year. The mechanics are unforgiving. Section 125(5.1) links eligibility for the full SBD to how much passive investment income the CCPC and its associated group earns each year, and the rule creates a sliding scale where excess passive income chips away at the business limit dollar by dollar. Specifically, the deduction grinds by five dollars for every one dollar of adjusted aggregate investment income above $50,000 in the associated group's prior year, and is completely eliminated at $150,000. This is not theoretical for Winnipeg clinics. Think of a physician with $2 million invested, or a lawyer whose holding company has been quietly growing for a decade. Because the CRA, the Canada Revenue Agency, measures last year's number, there is no fixing it once the year closes. If a client is near the threshold, this is the month to discuss a holding company split, though tread carefully. Moving passive investments into a holding company while keeping operations in a separate operating company is meant to separate passive income from the corporation claiming the SBD, but CRA anti-avoidance rules under subsection 125(5.2) are specifically designed to address structures created primarily to reduce that passive income. For many clients, the simpler move is redirecting new corporate cash toward personal RRSP and TFSA room instead of letting it pile up inside the company. On the registered plan side generally, nothing new landed from CRA this week on FHSA, RESP, or TFSA limits, so no changes to those numbers for now.

On regulation, the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, or CIRO, banned a former BMO Investments mutual fund representative after a hearing panel accepted a settlement over unauthorized trades, with Wealth Professional reporting the rep admitted altering Know Your Client data and then refused a CIRO interview. Separately, Investment Executive reports CIRO's own operating costs are projected to rise 10% this fiscal year to 188.2 million dollars, largely tied to cybersecurity spending after last August's breach, with member fees climbing 6.3% to cover it. Expect some of that passed through by your dealer.

On the business side, Richardson Wealth is disappearing as a name. The Globe and Mail reports the firm will rebrand as Nobelia Wealth on November 30th, under new parent iA Financial, which closed its 597 million dollar acquisition of the firm last October. Elsewhere, Wellington-Altus added an advisor team in Saint John, and in Cambridge, Ontario, Wealth Professional reports a 36 year advisory practice carrying nearly 300 households has left its dealer entirely to launch as an independent portfolio manager. Same pattern all year: established teams trading dealer platforms for full discretionary control.

On product, fixed income is still adjusting to the scars of 2022, with Wealth Professional reporting providers reshaping bond lineups around demand for shorter duration and more flexibility. On insurance, Advisor.ca cites AM Best data showing Canadian life and annuity sales hit a record 2.3 billion dollars in 2025, though the report flags a persistent coverage gap, useful context for any insurance needs conversation this month.

A few more for your notes. Prime Minister Carney is opening Toronto Pearson and three other hubs to private capital, with Ottawa keeping ownership while investors operate for decades, Wealth Professional reports. That fits a new Marsh survey of 430 asset owners showing infrastructure and emerging markets topping global wish lists. In the US, the Securities and Exchange Commission cleared tokenized stock trading under a five year exemption requiring dividend and voting rights, nothing changes on a Canadian platform yet, but expect client questions. And in Alberta, a court struck a First Nation's fraud claim against a councillor after the Nation tried to abandon a losing motion, a reminder that governance disputes are increasingly landing in court.

For clients in transition, the Globe's piece on a retiree's first year out of the workforce is worth sharing, the person spent more than expected and leaned harder on their financial plan than expected. And the Globe's look at momentum investing is a good one for anyone chasing hot ETFs right now, momentum works until it reverses fast. If you have Ontario clients, MoneySense reports consumer insolvencies there are rising faster than the rest of the country, and Ontario's new rental rules on evictions and late payments took effect September 21st.
talkingPoints: Manitoba froze its own tax brackets this year, so bracket creep costs filers real money even with no rate change.
If your corporation earned passive income in 2025, it is already shaping your small business deduction for 2026.
Watch Macklem's Halifax remarks today, an October hike is now on the table, not just a hold.
Richardson Wealth becomes Nobelia Wealth on November 30th, expect client questions about statements and branding.
Financial stress and health issues are showing up together, ask clients directly how they are doing, not just their portfolio.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Manitoba's Deficit Shrinks, Hydro Faces Gas Pushback
blocks.script:
Manitoba's public accounts are out, and the province's deficit for the year that just closed lands at 832 million dollars, about half the 1.66 billion dollar shortfall the government forecast back in December. The Free Press quotes officials calling it "moving in the right direction," and the provincial government now says Manitoba is on track to balance the budget next year. For anyone tracking the province's credit picture, that's a real swing, driven by revenue that came in stronger than assumed. It lands the same week a new Free Press, Abacus Data poll shows Premier Wab Kinew's New Democratic Party climbing to its highest support level yet province wide, while the Progressive Conservatives under Obby Khan lose further ground. Good fiscal news and good polling news arriving together tends to make a government bolder heading into next spring's budget, not more cautious.

On the civic side, incumbent mayor Scott Gillingham used a city hall news conference Monday to propose a new chief growth officer position at City Hall, modeled on the chief construction officer role he already created. Gillingham said he would create a new office within the administration focused on economic development, led by a chief growth officer, because the city needs a strong economy to deliver the services people depend on. The role would act as a liaison between the city, surrounding municipalities and the provincial government, as well as on trade missions arranged by organizations such as Winnipeg Economic Development and Tourism. Chris Lorenc of the Manitoba Heavy Construction Association stood with him, pointing to the CentrePort South file as the kind of project that needed this kind of senior attention years ago. This is an election pitch, growth and investment attraction framed as core city business ahead of next month's municipal vote.

Also on the municipal file, Transcona councillor Russ Wyatt filed to seek re-election Monday, one day ahead of the nomination deadline, despite facing sexual assault charges. CBC reports he filed his paperwork at city hall like any other candidate. That race will be one of the more closely watched contests when ballots are counted next month.

Manitoba Hydro is on your watch list, and there's real news there. Six weeks of Public Utilities Board hearings into Hydro's long term generating plan wrapped up earlier this month, and closing arguments included groups asserting Manitoba Hydro failed to demonstrate its long-held claim it might run out of power during midwinter cold snaps by 2030, and questioning the need for three natural gas turbines and whether they can indeed be bought for 3 billion dollars. A lawyer with the Public Interest Law Centre, representing a coalition of consumer groups, said there's no credible load forecast behind the electricity increase projections. That 3 billion dollar Brandon expansion has already been complicated by the trade war, since the turbines were meant to come from a Massachusetts manufacturer. This is a live file for anyone with Hydro bond exposure or industrial clients thinking about future rate pressure, the board's recommendation is still to come.

A run of serious public safety stories too, the kind clients will ask about. Clayton Herman, a Winnipeg born man, is back in Canada after nine and a half months in a California immigration detention centre. CBC reports he described poor food, mould on the walls and a lack of proper medical care while held there as a Canadian citizen. A former Winnipeg Catholic school teacher was sentenced to nine months in jail for repeatedly messaging a teenage student that he loved her, and the judge's line, "she was a child," is the one making headlines this morning. A U.S. court will hear an appeal next month from a man convicted in the smuggling case that led to a family of four freezing to death trying to walk across the Manitoba border into Minnesota. In West Kildonan, a 19 year old man faces impaired driving charges after police say a stolen SUV he was driving went airborne, rolled, and killed a 20 year old woman Sunday, leaving another woman with life threatening injuries. In Portage la Prairie, a high school and nearby daycares were locked down Monday after a 14 year old boy was stabbed by another teen and taken to hospital in Winnipeg. In Lynn Lake, Royal Canadian Mounted Police are investigating after a 72 year old man died outside their own detachment Sunday morning, in what they're calling a suspected homicide. And Winnipeg police say they're increasing patrols around the city's worship centres after Sunday's shooting outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, that wounded a man and a police officer.

On the weather and economy front, forecasters say a strengthening El Niño could bring one of the strongest winter patterns on record to the Prairies, which matters for farm income and heating costs across rural Manitoba. In Ottawa, Parliament's fall sitting opened with a rowdy question period and a new major projects bill from the Carney government, part of the response to a trade fight that's already squeezing farm margins here. In Saskatchewan, the two pilots killed in last week's plane crash near Kisbey have been identified by India's consulate as flight school students Manoj Sivakumar and Srisaran Thirugnanasambantham. And in Quebec, a crowded field of five parties has left voters lukewarm two weeks before an October 5th election.

Two more names on your watch list. The Winnipeg Jets beat the Colorado Avalanche 3 to 1 in preseason play at Canada Life Centre Monday night, with new starter Stuart Skinner stopping 31 shots in his Jets debut. And the Winnipeg Blue Bombers had quarterback Zach Collaros miss his first practice back from the bye week with a head injury, with backup Bryce Brown taking the reps while the team waits to see if Collaros is ready for the next game.
talkingPoints: Manitoba's deficit came in at half the forecast, 832 million versus 1.66 billion, and the province says it's on track to balance next year.
Gillingham wants a chief growth officer at City Hall, an election year pitch to centralize economic development ahead of next month's vote.
Manitoba Hydro's Brandon gas turbine expansion is facing real pushback at the Public Utilities Board over cost and need.
Watch the Transcona council race, Russ Wyatt is running again while facing sexual assault charges.
Jets opened preseason with a win behind new goalie Stuart Skinner, Bombers are watching Zach Collaros's head injury closely.

blocks.title: Ottawa's Fall Sitting: Pipelines, Poilievre, and NATO Money
blocks.script:
The federal government is now formally offering money to First Nations along the Trans Mountain pipeline route, and the number is worth knowing: $2.5 million per First Nation that signs onto an equity stake in the pipeline. The Globe and Mail reports some Indigenous leaders say the offer falls short of what they expected when Ottawa first floated giving communities a real ownership piece of the pipeline it bought back in 2018. For clients with exposure to pipeline debt or energy infrastructure funds, this is the mechanism Ottawa is using to try to lock in social license before more capacity comes online. Worth watching whether uptake is broad, or whether this becomes another flashpoint.

blocks.label: Climate Policy & Nonprofit Governance
blocks.title: Energy Crisis Deepens as Climate Rules Roll Back
blocks.script:
Good morning. Today's climate policy roundup covers a world leaders' summit shadowed by an energy crisis, rollbacks to US power plant rules, and a notable court win for young Canadians suing over climate policy.

World leaders are gathering this week at the United Nations General Assembly, with the Associated Press reporting that climate shocks and rising prices are compounding fears about war, division, and runaway artificial intelligence. The future of the UN itself is expected to be part of the conversation, alongside speculation over who might become the next secretary general.

The energy crisis triggered by conflict in the Middle East is dominating policy discussions. The Financial Times reports that French President Emmanuel Macron has called for a G7 summit to consider releasing more strategic oil reserves, as a previous coordinated release from earlier this year nears completion. Macron also said he wants to coordinate a European Union-wide response on natural gas supplies, including boosting storage levels.

Meanwhile, Reuters reports that EU finance ministers met last week to discuss a possible windfall tax on energy company profits, with further talks expected in October. The Guardian notes that with elections due next year in several EU countries, leaders are moving to get ahead of what analysts warn could be one of the continent's biggest energy shocks in decades. Governments from Germany to Bangladesh have already adjusted fuel taxes and prices in response to the turmoil, according to Reuters and Politico.

In the United States, Canary Media reports that the Environmental Protection Agency has significantly weakened climate rules for power plants, and the outlet examines what that means for the electricity sector going forward. Separately, the Washington Post reports a judge has ruled that Trump's EPA must reinstate a seven billion dollar grant program for solar panels.

On carbon removal, Heatmap's Emily Pontecorvo reports from New York Climate Week that industry voices, including Senator Brian Schatz of Hawaii, struck an optimistic tone despite the difficult political climate. Schatz pointed to a nearly one billion dollar fund pledged by carbon removal buyers group Frontier Climate, and to continued bipartisan support in Congress for the 45Q tax credit. Panelists including Frontier's Joanna Klitzke argued the industry should be transparent about failed projects to build credibility with skeptics, while Clean Economy Project cofounder Cristina Shoffer stressed the importance of building relationships with lawmakers ahead of the November midterms.

On the governance side, Canada's National Observer reports that a Federal Court judge has rejected a bid to dismiss a youth-led climate lawsuit against the federal government over its 2030 climate plan, clearing the way for the case, known as the Mathur case, to proceed.

Also in Canada, the Philanthropist Journal highlights the launch of Democracy Funders Canada, a new national network of foundations formed to strengthen philanthropy's role in supporting pluralist democracy at a time the group's steering committee says Canadian democratic institutions are under stress.

And in the Guardian, a comment piece from Damian Carrington and colleagues examines how Saudi Arabian oil scientists came to be involved in authoring some of the world's most influential climate reports through the IPCC process.
talkingPoints: One, the Middle East conflict is reshaping global energy policy, with France pushing for a G7-coordinated release of oil reserves and the EU debating a windfall profits tax on energy firms.
Two, the Trump administration continues to unwind federal climate regulation, with the EPA weakening power plant rules even as a court forces reinstatement of a solar grant program.
Three, the carbon removal industry is trying to broaden political support ahead of the midterms, leaning on bipartisan tax credit survival and private funding commitments.
Four, a Canadian court has allowed a youth climate lawsuit against the federal government to move forward, a notable development in climate litigation.
Five, a new philanthropic network, Democracy Funders Canada, has launched specifically to bolster nonprofit and foundation support for democratic institutions.

blocks.label: AI & Technology
blocks.title: Math Machines, Blocked Agents, and Skeptical Retailers
blocks.script:
The biggest AI story today is what happens after a model gets too good, too fast. OpenAI has formed an independent advisory group of nine mathematicians, hosted at Princeton's Institute for Advanced Study, after an internal model resolved more than 100 additional open problems across most areas of mathematics. That follows the abrupt publication of a solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem. Many prominent mathematicians have taken issue with the frenzied pace of those results, and earlier this month twenty-five Fields Medal winning mathematicians signed an open letter arguing that AI labs are threatening their intellectual work. The new group can speak publicly, but it won't be given leeway to slow down or redirect OpenAI's ongoing mathematical research. The signal for you: a research model is now outpacing credentialed experts in their own specialty, and even OpenAI needed outside referees to manage the fallout.

Ben Thompson at Stratechery argues Anthropic's public case for "pacing the frontier," slowing capability gains for safety, conveniently buys the company time on a real problem: models are improving faster than the tooling wrapped around them. His point is that profit flows to whoever owns the integration between model and software harness, which is why Microsoft repositioned itself as a neutral harness provider after its OpenAI relationship cooled. He also notes that once you count training costs properly, Anthropic is solidly profitable, useful if clients ask whether this buildout is a bubble.

The agent wars turned physical this week. Meta's shopping agent Muse has out-downloaded ChatGPT's early mobile launch in the US and Canada, per TechCrunch citing Appfigures. Amazon responded by blocking it outright, saying Muse never disclosed itself while browsing and was capturing customer login credentials, a real fraud exposure if a client ever lets a shopping bot log into a retail account. Amazon is already suing Perplexity for similar behaviour. The strategic read from Thompson this morning: owning warehouses and delivery planes may matter more in an AI economy than owning the chat app, because agents are easy to build and physical logistics are not.

Not everyone is sold on agentic shopping. Ron Johnson, who built Apple's retail stores under Steve Jobs, told TechCrunch "I don't know that it's going to change which way we shop," especially for anything over a thousand dollars, because buyers still want to hold a laptop before they pay for it. For all his skepticism about how AI will reshape shopping, Johnson remains bullish on the technology itself, calling himself a real believer and an AI optimist. Worth flagging for clients holding retail names: agentic commerce isn't unanimous even among people who built the physical version.

Google is selling a laptop called the Googlebook, starting at 899 dollars, built to showcase Gemini in the cursor, dictation, and desktop widgets. It's a bet people will replace a working laptop just for better AI baked into the operating system.

Closer to your own desk, TechCrunch profiled Tabby, a real-time bookkeeping tool built by a former accountant, handling client paperwork and profit-and-loss tracking without a human doing the entries. It's AI moving up the value chain in professional services, worth a ready answer next time a client asks who's next.

On Canadian tech, BetaKit reports a few raises worth knowing. Beacon, a roll-up of small software firms, bought New York's Haize Labs to help its portfolio companies deploy AI they can trust, a sign AI reliability testing is becoming its own business. Toronto's Altis Labs raised 25 million US dollars to expand AI for cancer trials. Calgary's Kanin Energy raised 138 million dollars for waste heat to power projects, relevant given how much electricity AI data centres are pulling off the grid. And Innovation Saskatchewan put another 300 thousand dollars into its AgTech Accelerator through 2028.

Last one, on accountability. MIT Technology Review published a fifteen-month investigation into US border surveillance towers, finding people died within range of cameras built to detect them. It's a US story, but it's the clearest case study going for how regulators here and abroad are thinking about AI: the gap between what a vendor claims a system can do and what it does in the field.
talkingPoints: OpenAI's math model now beats specialists at their own game, and OpenAI needed outside referees to manage it.
Amazon just blocked Meta's Muse agent over stolen login credentials, a live fraud risk in agentic shopping.

blocks.label: Health & Fitness
blocks.title: Outside Online's Fall Fitness and Gear Roundup
blocks.script:
Good day, and welcome to your Health and Fitness update for September 22nd, 2026. Today we're looking at a handful of stories from Outside Online focused on staying active, moving well, and gearing up for the fall season.

Let's start with something practical. Outside Online published a five minute stretch routine designed to relieve tight joints and a stiff back. The idea, according to the outlet, is a quick full body reset that helps people get back to the outdoor activities they enjoy, without needing a long recovery session. For anyone dealing with the aches that come from hiking, running, or just sitting too much, this kind of short routine is meant to be an easy addition to a daily routine.

On the gear side, Outside Online's team put together a list of the hiking boots and trail runners they consider standouts, currently available through REI's September sale. The gear team narrowed it down to thirteen favorites, spanning boots and trail running shoes, giving hikers a curated starting point as they gear up for fall trail season.

Sticking with running, Outside Online also reviewed the Salomon Aero Blaze 4 GRVL, a shoe built for gravel running. The reviewer admitted going in skeptical, comparing gravel shoes to a niche trend, but came away convinced after testing the Salomon model. It's a reminder that footwear built for mixed terrain is becoming a real category, not just a gimmick.

Zooming out to performance apparel more broadly, Outside Online explored whether high-tech clothing actually makes a measurable difference for athletes. The piece uses the world's first sub-two-hour marathon as a jumping off point, asking whether that kind of achievement signals a new era of performance apparel, or whether the gains are more about the athlete than the gear.

For those planning outdoor fitness activities this fall, Outside Online also put together a roundup of weekend adventure ideas, aimed at helping people fill their calendar with active pursuits as the weather cools.

And if travel is part of your fitness plans, the outlet highlighted seven under the radar ski towns around the country, describing them as down to earth alternatives to crowded resort destinations, with a local, affordable mountain town feel once winter arrives.

That's the roundup for today. The throughline across all of it is simple: whether it's a quick stretch, the right pair of shoes, or picking a good destination, small choices add up when it comes to staying active and feeling good doing it.

blocks.label: Parenting
blocks.title: Landlines Return, Paediatric Screen Guidance, and Parent Benefits
blocks.script:
Millennial parents are fixing a mistake from the last decade, and the fix looks like something from 1985. The Globe and Mail reports that Canadian families are turning to landlines, not smartphones, for the first phone they give their kids. A Toronto mom named Karlina Bear says there’s a whole movement happening in Canada to help give kids the privilege of having a smartphone-free childhood, tied to a group called Unplugged Canada. Bear is a parent champion at her school for Unplugged Canada, a national organization that encourages parents to delay giving smartphones to kids until they’re at least 14. Instead, parents are buying devices like the Tin Can, a Wi-Fi landline with parental controls. It's a parent-controlled home phone that has already sold hundreds of thousands of units in Canada and the U.S. since the Seattle-based startup launched last year.

That instinct lines up with the paediatric evidence. According to the Canadian Paediatric Society's guidelines, screen time for children younger than 2 years is not recommended, while screen time for children aged 2 to 5 should be limited to one hour or less per day. For school age children, the recent recommendations are based on the four essential Ms model: managing screen time, meaningful screen time use, modeling healthy use, and monitoring for problematic screen use.

If a client has a new baby, three levers matter. Employment Insurance parental leave lets a couple split up to forty weeks of standard benefits, or sixty one weeks extended. The Canada Child Benefit is indexed every July, worth checking on a client's latest notice. And the Registered Education Savings Plan still gets a twenty percent federal top up on contributions, up to five hundred dollars a year, so encourage new parents to open one early.

One line for your own day: the Globe's horoscope for September 22 favours practical decisions today, useful if this comes up with a client.
talkingPoints: Kids are getting landlines before smartphones, part of a delay-to-fourteen movement in Canada.
Canadian Paediatric Society still says no screens under two, one hour max for ages two to five.
Older kids: it is about managing, meaning, modelling, and monitoring, not a hard time cap.
New parents can split parental leave up to forty weeks standard or sixty one extended.
RESP contributions still get a twenty percent government top-up, so open one early.

blocks.label: Sports
blocks.title: Babcock's Back, Bombers Host Argos Friday
blocks.script:
The Winnipeg Jets are on your watch list, and the biggest hockey story touching them today is about a coach on another bench. Mike Babcock is back in the National Hockey League running the Edmonton Oilers, and the Globe and Mail says his return is the headline off-season coaching change across the league. That matters here because Edmonton is a Central Division rival, so the Jets will see plenty of Babcock's team this year.

The Blue Bombers, also on your watch list, are part of the Canadian Football League, the CFL. The Blue Bombers sit at a record of seven wins and six losses, fourth in the West Division. They host the Toronto Argonauts Friday, September 25th, at 8 PM Eastern, a game that matters for playoff seeding as the regular season winds down.

Staying in hockey, Jennifer Botterill, the Winnipeg product stepping into a broadcast role on TNT's NHL coverage, has a new memoir out. The Free Press says her book leans on a mantra that's already resonating in women's sports, and it doubles as a look behind the curtain at her years with Sportsnet.

Washington's Alex Ovechkin is day to day with a lower body injury, per the Globe and Mail, with the Capitals opening their season October 2nd at Carolina. In Vancouver, forward Cotter is trying to carve out a role with a Canucks team still deep in a rebuild. In Edmonton, defenceman Bouchard, last year's top scoring blueliner on that roster, says he'd rather answer his critics directly than let the noise sit.

On the other end, the Carolina Hurricanes are the reigning Stanley Cup champion, and the Globe's off-season look says no team has won more games than Carolina since Rod Brind'Amour took over in 2018, yet their style is proving hard for the rest of the league to copy. Elsewhere in roster movement, Sergei Bobrovsky signed with the Maple Leafs after backstopping Florida to consecutive Stanley Cups, and owns a career .912 save percentage. Brady Tkachuk is now a Panther after requesting a trade out of Ottawa, joining his brother Matthew in Florida, and Brendan Gallagher was dealt to Vancouver after spending his entire career with Montreal.

Over in the National Football League, injuries are the story. The Giants lost rookie quarterback Jaxson Dart to a knee injury in a loss to the Rams, and also saw pass rusher Brian Burns sprain an ankle and left tackle Andrew Thomas go down, per the Globe. In Chicago, coach Ben Johnson said Monday that Caleb Williams, hurt with a hamstring, will be week to week but appears to have avoided serious damage. In Washington, Jayden Daniels dislocated his elbow again in a loss to Dallas, a bigger worry for that franchise. On the good side, Kansas City improved to two and oh, with Kenneth Walker the third changing the math in that backfield and Patrick Mahomes making defences pay in an overtime win over Indianapolis. And Bill Belichick keeps making headlines at North Carolina, with the Globe asking directly whether the turmoil around that program is worth it.

In the National Basketball Association, the Raptors signed guard Jaden Bradley to a multi-year deal after he averaged better than thirteen points a game at Arizona last season. The Clippers named John Gibson interim chief executive and governor after Steve Ballmer's ban from the league. And in the Women's National Basketball Association, the final week of the regular season still has the playoff picture muddled, with Minnesota-Indiana and New York-Atlanta among the games to watch.

Quickly around the rest of the world: soccer's governing body, FIFA, says its president is open to outside review of how the organization makes decisions. A Belgian cyclist was hit by a driver while training near Montreal and is out of the road world championships there. Ottawa's Gabriela Dabrowski won her fourth WTA doubles title of the season in Brazil. And in Calgary, the Crown withdrew fraud charges against former Cricket Canada chief executive Salman Khan.

No Jets or Bombers action tonight. NHL preseason continues around the league, and the WNBA regular season keeps grinding toward its final games this week.

blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: CPP: how the benefit is calculated, the enhancement, and the take it early or late decision / Delivering bad news: the structure that keeps trust
blocks.script:
Financial Planning Facts, lesson 8: CPP: how the benefit is calculated, the enhancement, and the take it early or late decision.

CPP, the Canada Pension Plan, pays you a percentage of your average pensionable earnings, worked out over your contributory period from age 18 until you start your pension. Since 2019, Ottawa has been phasing in the enhancement, which lifts the replacement rate from 25% of average earnings up to 33%, and adds a second tier called CPP2 on earnings above the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings, or YMPE. For 2026, that YMPE is $74,900. The additional ceiling for CPP2, the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings, is $83,900. If your income sits above $74,900 in 2026, you and your employer each pay an extra 4% into CPP2 on the slice up to $83,900. That extra contribution buys extra pension later.

Now the decision that actually matters: when to start. Standard age is 65. Take it at 60, and it's cut 0.6% for every month before 65, that's 36% less, for life. Wait to 70, it grows 0.7% for every month after 65, that's 42% more, for life.

Here's the math. Say your CPP at 65 would be $1,300 a month, close to the 2025 maximum of $1,364.60. Start at 60, you get roughly $832 a month for life. Wait to 70, you get roughly $1,846 a month for life. The break even point, where delaying overtakes starting early in total dollars received, lands around age 74. Live past 74, delaying wins. Die before 74, starting early wins.

The one mistake: people decide based on a gut feeling about how long they'll live, without checking family longevity, their spouse's income needs, or whether they're still working and paying into CPP2 anyway. Incorporated business owners especially keep working past 65, which changes the math because they're still contributing and still earning other income that stacks on top.

Your task, under fifteen minutes: pull your latest CPP Statement of Contributions from your My Service Canada Account, find your estimated pension at 65, then calculate what it would be at 60 and at 70 using the percentages above.

Communication, lesson 8: Delivering bad news: the structure that keeps trust.

In 2000, Dr. Walter Baile at MD Anderson published a protocol called SPIKES for oncologists telling patients their cancer had returned. Before SPIKES, doctors were rated by patients as cold or evasive nearly half the time, per the study in The Oncologist. The fix wasn't more empathy training. It was sequence. Setting, then Perception, then Invitation, then Knowledge, then Emotion, then Summary. The headline comes fourth, but it comes clearly, in one sentence, before anything softens it.

Advisors get this backwards. Say a client's portfolio dropped 22 percent in 2022, versus the S&P 500's 18 percent decline that year, per Morningstar data. The instinct is to open with the Fed, inflation, the bond market, three minutes of context, and only then say the number. By the time the number lands, the client has stopped listening for the point and started scanning for the excuse. Trust erodes not because the news is bad, but because they had to hunt for it.

The structure that works: state the fact in one sentence first. "Your account is down 22 percent this year." Then check what they already understand. Then explain the mechanism briefly. Then name the emotion out loud, something like "I know that number is hard to sit with." Then summarize what happens next, concretely. Baile's data showed patients rated doctors as more trustworthy when bad news came early and plainly, even though the news itself didn't change.

The one mistake: leading with reasons instead of the result. Reasons before results reads as defense. Results before reasons reads as respect.

Your task today: pull up the last piece of bad financial or project news you delivered to a client or board. Rewrite the opening two sentences so the fact comes first, no qualifier, no cushion. Time yourself, this takes under ten minutes.

blocks.label: Markets & Economy
blocks.title: Markets Rally as Tech Surges, Oil Retreats
blocks.script:
Good morning. Global markets opened the week higher today, buoyed by a rally in technology stocks and a pullback in oil prices, according to Bloomberg and the Globe and Mail's Before the Bell newsletter.

Wall Street futures pointed higher after a mixed close on Friday. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 futures were both up around one percent in early trading, according to Bloomberg's Morning Briefing. In Europe, the pan-European STOXX 600 climbed more than one percent, with Britain's FTSE 100, Germany's DAX and France's CAC 40 all posting solid gains. In Asia, Hong Kong's Hang Seng rose more than one percent, though Japanese markets were closed for a holiday.

The rally comes as investors look ahead to this week's summit between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Bloomberg reports that US and Chinese officials described talks on artificial intelligence, trade and investment as constructive, with the two sides agreeing to launch an AI dialogue, even though they failed to extend their existing trade truce. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called the discussions "very successful."

Oil prices helped calm investor nerves after spiking last week. Brent crude fell more than two percent, trading around 100 to 101 dollars a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate dropped close to three percent. The Globe and Mail reports that some of the anxiety that rattled markets last week over fears of a global central bank hiking cycle has eased as oil pulls back from highs above 109 dollars a barrel seen just days earlier. IG chief market strategist Chris Beauchamp said the move looks like a correction rather than a change in the underlying trend, which he still sees pointing higher over time.

Traders are also watching for diplomatic progress on the Iran war. Bloomberg notes that Trump said he may meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of this week's UN General Assembly meetings, fueling hopes that tensions in the region could ease. Still, strains in energy markets remain visible elsewhere. US retail diesel prices topped six dollars and fifty cents a gallon for the first time, Bloomberg reports, and the ongoing standoff in the Black Sea is raising concerns about a potential food supply shock.

Gold slipped alongside the broader shift toward risk assets. Spot gold was down around half a percent, trading near 4,350 dollars an ounce, according to the Globe and Mail.

In currency markets, the Canadian dollar weakened slightly against its US counterpart, trading in a range of roughly 71.3 to 71.5 US cents. The loonie is down about a quarter of a percent over the past month. The US dollar index ticked up modestly.

On the bond side, the yield on the US 10-year Treasury note eased to just under 5 percent.

The AI investment boom remains a dominant force in markets. Bloomberg's Markets Daily newsletter points out that AI-related spending now accounts for roughly half of US GDP growth by some estimates, and nearly 33 trillion dollars in market value has been added to the S&P 500 since late 2022, with most of that gain tied to AI-linked companies. Jim Morrow of Callodine Capital Management warned that markets and the broader economy are so intertwined with AI right now that a slowdown could unravel a great deal, and that fund managers are finding it hard to diversify away from AI exposure even across private equity, corporate bonds and Treasuries.

That AI wave shows no sign of slowing. SoftBank is reportedly seeking to raise more than 11 billion dollars in what would be one of the largest junk bond deals ever, as it ramps up investment in OpenAI, according to Bloomberg. Meanwhile Citigroup chief executive Jane Fraser said companies are racing to bolster their defenses as increasingly powerful AI models raise the risk of cyberattacks.

Individual stock moves reflected some of these AI-driven currents. Accenture gained more than six percent in premarket trading after Anthropic partnered with the firm to test the safety of its advanced AI models. Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount Skydance also rose sharply on signs of progress in settlement talks with California officials over Paramount's planned acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, a deal Bloomberg says now includes discussions over theatrical release commitments and keeping major operations in California.

Not every story was upbeat. Bloomberg's Markets Daily newsletter recapped a meltdown in Turkey's stock market last week, where regulators cracked down on funds suspected of artificially inflating illiquid stocks. Asset manager Tera's chairman has been arrested and executives' assets frozen, and the chairman of finance company Destek, whose fortune had ballooned to nearly 14 billion dollars on the back of Tera's investments, has also been detained. Analyst Murat Gulkan warned that the seized, thinly traded shares could fetch only "pennies on the dollar" if sold off.

In Europe, tens of thousands of workers at Volkswagen and other German carmakers protested against factory closures, Bloomberg reports, after VW slashed its profit forecast on Friday.

North of the border, the Globe and Mail notes that Canadian construction investment figures for July are due today, and Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem is scheduled to speak in Halifax. In Ottawa, Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon acknowledged, according to The Peak newsletter, that the federal government cannot guarantee air travel costs won't rise once Canada's largest airports are opened to private investors, even as fees remain partially regulated.

On the corporate calendar, Costco and BlackBerry are both due to report earnings this week, along with General Mills and H&M, offering fresh signals on consumer spending heading into the fall.
talkingPoints: One, global stocks rallied to start the week as AI optimism and retreating oil prices lifted sentiment, though strategists caution the drop in oil looks like a pause rather than a reversal of the broader upward trend.
Two, all eyes are on this week's Trump-Xi summit, with both sides striking a constructive tone on AI and trade even after failing to extend their existing tariff truce.

Three, the scale of AI-driven market gains, estimated near 33 trillion dollars in added S&P 500 value since 2022, is prompting warnings from fund managers that diversification strategies may no longer protect investors if the AI boom slows.
Four, Turkey's fund crisis, with arrests, frozen assets and plunging share prices, is a reminder of the risks tied to illiquid, high-flying investment vehicles.

Five, in Canada, attention turns to construction investment data and comments from Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem, along with questions about airport privatization and its potential effect on travel costs.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Cameco, Nvidia And Xanadu Lead The Ten
blocks.script:
Start with Cameco, the Saskatoon-based uranium miner that supplies fuel and services to nuclear utilities around the world. The Globe and Mail reports Cameco shareholders are expected to share in the company's massive win on an investment in Westinghouse Electric Co., with the Saskatoon-based uranium miner poised to boost dividends after a planned Westinghouse initial public offering, which analysts estimate will value the company at between US thirty billion and fifty billion dollars. The tailwind is nuclear demand itself, with utilities around the world having ordered up to 91 of its flagship Advanced Passive 1000 reactors for delivery over the next two decades. Cameco already doubled its own dividend from twelve cents to twenty four cents a share between 2023 and 2025, a year ahead of its own target. The headwind is that Westinghouse's earnings boost won't immediately translate into equivalent cash flow for Cameco, since large non-cash amortization charges and debt servicing take priority over dividend distributions. An evidence-based advisor would tell you a dividend story riding on one subsidiary's IPO timing is worth tracking, not a reason to load up on a single mining stock.

Stay with that same story for Westinghouse, the nuclear reactor manufacturer that went bankrupt once and was bought out of Toshiba's hands by Brookfield back in 2018. It is now heading toward a US listing this fall, with at least five investment banks hired to lead the offering, according to Bloomberg. The tailwind is a genuine global nuclear buildout that gives it real order books, not just investor enthusiasm. The headwind is roughly four billion dollars of debt a public listing needs to help recapitalize before profits flow freely to its owners. An evidence-based advisor would say this is a private-to-public transition worth watching for what it signals about nuclear financing generally, not something a retail client can act on before shares actually price.

Third, Brookfield Renewable Partners, the renewable power arm of Brookfield Corp that holds the majority stake in Westinghouse alongside Cameco. Brookfield Renewable owns a 51 per cent stake in Westinghouse and Cameco holds 49 per cent, so Brookfield stands to see the largest dollar gain if that IPO prices anywhere near current estimates. The tailwind is diversification, with nuclear exposure sitting alongside its wind, solar and hydro assets. The headwind is complexity, since unit holders are effectively betting on execution of a subsidiary's listing layered on top of Brookfield's core renewable business. An evidence-based advisor would say Brookfield's structure rewards patient, diversified holders and punishes anyone trying to trade around a single asset sale.

Fourth, Nvidia, the American chipmaker that dominates the market for processors powering artificial intelligence. It is in the news because chief executive Jensen Huang pushed back hard on what the BBC calls doomsday narratives, rejecting warnings from AI researchers that the technology could lead to human extinction. The tailwind remains enormous AI infrastructure spending that keeps flowing toward its chips from every major cloud provider. The headwind is that Huang's comments land right as scrutiny of AI safety and concentration risk in a handful of mega-cap suppliers keeps building among regulators and investors alike. An evidence-based advisor would tell a client that one chief executive dismissing existential risk is not investment analysis, and that Nvidia's valuation already prices in a lot of good news continuing indefinitely.

Fifth, Xanadu, the Toronto quantum computing developer that went public six months ago. The Globe reports its lockup lifts on September twenty second, freeing most investor and insider shares to trade for the first time since the listing. The tailwind is being one of Canada's few pure-play quantum computing stocks in a sector pulling global attention and capital. The headwind is straightforward supply and demand: when a large batch of previously locked shares suddenly becomes tradeable, prices often soften on the extra volume regardless of how the underlying business is doing. An evidence-based advisor would tell a client that lockup expiries are a well-documented, mechanical pattern, not a referendum on the technology, and that trading around this specific date is speculation dressed up as a thesis.

Sixth, Manchester United, the English football club now caught up in an ownership controversy. The BBC reports its billionaire owner says he has lost confidence in the UK over high taxes and immigration and has moved into tax exile, prompting a Labour committee chair to say he has lost the moral high ground. The tailwind for the club commercially is that its global brand keeps generating sponsorship and broadcast revenue almost regardless of who owns it. The headwind is reputational, with ownership controversy feeding fan and political anger that can complicate stadium and investment decisions down the line. An evidence-based advisor would say ownership dramas at sports clubs rarely move the numbers that actually matter inside a diversified portfolio.

Seventh, Hyundai, the Korean automaker. CBC reports a Santa Fe SUV caught fire on a busy highway just after dealership repairs, with the owner, Jason Pelletier, still waiting three months later for answers and full compensation. The tailwind for Hyundai is that its North American sales and market share have held up well through past recall cycles. The headwind is exactly this kind of story, since a vehicle fire tied to post-repair work raises fresh questions about dealership quality control and how the warranty process actually treats customers. An evidence-based advisor would say a single-incident recall story rarely changes an automaker's long-term investment case, but it is worth watching if a pattern of similar claims starts to build.

Eighth, and last for this segment, Korn Ferry, the global workforce consulting firm. The Globe cites its latest research finding nearly half of workers say they are too busy to deliver meaningful results, juggling multiple roles as artificial intelligence adds to workloads instead of easing them. The tailwind for Korn Ferry itself is steady demand for exactly this kind of workforce data as companies wrestle with productivity questions. The headwind is that the finding cuts against the growth story many corporate clients want to tell their own investors, which puts pressure on how those companies message their AI rollouts. An evidence-based advisor would say data like this is a good reason to ask any growth company how it actually measures output, not just headcount or activity.
talkingPoints: Cameco's dividend story depends on Westinghouse actually pricing its IPO this fall.
Xanadu's lockup lifts tomorrow, and that alone can move the stock.
Nvidia's chief executive dismissing extinction fears is not the same as derisking the stock.
Hyundai's fire claim is one incident so far, worth watching, not yet a pattern.
Ask any company touting AI productivity gains how they are actually measuring output.

blocks.title: Provinces Hold AA Ratings, Defence ETFs Launch
blocks.script:
Good day. Here's your industry and regulatory update for Monday, September 21st, 2026.

Fitch Ratings says five Canadian provinces have held onto their AA credit ratings despite mounting debt loads. According to a new report covered by Investment Executive and Advisor dot ca, the five rated provinces are now facing a divergence in their debt trajectories, meaning some are managing their finances more sustainably than others even as they keep the same overall grade for now.

In the product world, the exchange traded fund space is getting more crowded in the defence sector. Ninepoint and Evolve have both launched new defence focused ETFs, joining a wave of new offerings this month. Alongside those, TD Asset Management, CI Global Asset Management, Canada Life, and Caldwell have each rolled out new products, while Mackenzie and Franklin Templeton have made changes to existing funds. This continues a busy stretch for Canada's fund providers as they compete for investor dollars heading into the fall.

On the people side, Wellington-Altus has added an advisor team in Saint John, New Brunswick, expanding its East Coast presence. Other moves this week touched Designed, Harbourfront Wealth, BMO Financial, and Worldsource Wealth, according to Investment Executive and Advisor dot ca's weekly roundup of industry moves.

Turning to the broader backdrop shaping these decisions, Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem was in Halifax today speaking about economic developments, with a media availability following. The central bank held its overnight rate at 2.25 percent earlier this month, and investors are watching closely for signals on how policymakers are weighing a softening economy against renewed inflation pressure coming from oil prices and a weaker Canadian dollar.

Markets opened the week on a mixed but generally calmer note. The Toronto Stock Exchange dipped slightly on Friday, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq posted modest gains on a rally in technology stocks. Globally, European markets climbed on Monday morning, with the pan-European STOXX 600 up more than one percent, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng also higher, though Japanese markets were closed for a holiday.

Oil prices helped calm nerves after a volatile week. Brent crude slipped back toward the 100 dollar a barrel mark, down nearly three percent, as investors grew hopeful about diplomatic progress on the Iran conflict ahead of this week's United Nations meeting, and as Saudi shipments showed signs of a partial recovery despite ongoing attacks from Yemen's Houthis. Market strategists cautioned that the longer term direction for oil still points higher, calling last week's spike above 109 dollars a barrel an overreaction that is now correcting.

The Canadian dollar weakened against the U.S. dollar, trading near 1.40 to the greenback, continuing a slow slide over the past month. The U.S. ten year Treasury yield eased slightly but remains close to 5 percent, a level that has been drawing attention from bond markets. Gold prices pulled back as well.

On the industry data front, Canadian mutual fund and ETF assets hit new all time highs in August, according to figures from the Statistics and Investment Management Association, or SIMA, reported by Wealth Professional. Record fund assets and strong ETF sales point to sustained investor confidence heading into the fall.

Also from Wealth Professional, fixed mortgage rates rose in August even as home affordability improved in most Canadian markets. Falling home prices eased buying conditions for many, but climbing bond yields pushed fixed mortgage rates higher, a reminder that affordability gains on one side of the ledger can be offset by borrowing costs on the other.

On the merger and acquisition front, global M&A value rose 15 percent this year, with the financial sector showing the highest sentiment among dealmakers, according to Wealth Professional. Megadeals are surging, though small and mid-market transaction volumes remain well below historical norms. Separately, Swedish private equity giant EQT has raised its takeover bid for Australian asset manager Perpetual for a fourth time, with ambitions that reportedly extend into the Canadian advisor market.

Finally, a note of caution for consumers and advisors alike. A new study reported by Wealth Professional found that major AI chatbots gave wrong answers to financial questions in 57 percent of cases tested, raising serious questions about how much everyday Canadians should rely on artificial intelligence tools for financial advice.

Two, the ETF market is expanding fast in defence, with new launches from Ninepoint and Evolve joining a broader wave of new fund products this month.
