blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: BoC, Dollarama, Brookfield Lead Today's Company Watch
blocks.script:
Start with the Bank of Canada, because it is on the watch list and it is genuinely in the news today. This is the country's central bank, the body that sets the overnight interest rate eight times a year. The Bank of Canada maintained the target for its overnight rate unchanged at 2.25% in its September 2026 decision, as expected by markets, but flagged stronger upside risks to inflation. The Globe reports the newly released summary of deliberations shows the Governing Council is worried the trade war with Washington will chill household spending, business investment and hiring before the next meeting in late October. The tailwind is that underlying inflation has held close to target. The headwind is that policymakers themselves see the trade fight as the wildcard. An evidence based advisor tells a client the hold changes nothing about a properly built bond ladder, do not trade around it.

Next, Dollarama. This is the Montreal based discount retailer that sells almost everything for a few dollars or less, and it just raised its sales growth outlook. The Globe reports the company beat estimates and lifted its forecast even as it treats price increases as a last resort. The tailwind is a squeezed Canadian shopper trading down, which keeps foot traffic climbing. The headwind is rising cost pressure in the second half, on tariffs and freight, that the company says it will absorb rather than pass on immediately. An evidence based advisor would say a strong quarter from a consumer bellwether like this is useful economic data, not a reason to chase the stock.

Amazon is next. This is the global online retailer and warehouse operator that employs thousands across Canada, and it just raised warehouse wages by a dollar an hour nationwide. The Globe frames this as a response to ongoing union organizing attempts in multiple Canadian jurisdictions. The tailwind is that a wage bump defuses some organizing momentum heading into a contentious labour season. The headwind is that unionization pressure has not gone away and higher labour costs squeeze margins in a low margin logistics business. An evidence based advisor tells a client that a single company's labour headline rarely moves a diversified portfolio, and Amazon's weight there is already priced.

Now the big merger story. Brookfield is the Toronto based global alternative asset manager that invests pension and institutional money into infrastructure, real estate and industrials worldwide. Australia's Reliance Worldwide will back an almost US$2.9-billion buyout from global investment firm Brookfield, as the plumbing supplies company confronts the continuing impact of U.S. tariffs and economic uncertainty. The tailwind for Brookfield is a discounted entry point into a global industrial brand. The transaction also comes with a 30-day go-shop provision, allowing Reliance Worldwide to solicit and negotiate alternative proposals after signing the scheme implementation deed. That is the headwind, a rival bidder could still emerge. An advisor would note Brookfield's steady deal flow is a feature of the stock, not a one off catalyst.

On the other side of that deal sits Reliance Worldwide, the Australian maker of plumbing brands including SharkBite, which is agreeing to be taken private. Reliance depends on North America for the majority of its profit, where CEO Heath Sharp said the business's prospects had been hard hit by tariffs. The tailwind is certainty, shareholders get cash now instead of riding out a tariff hit. The headwind is that go shop window creating deal uncertainty for a few more weeks. An evidence based advisor tells a client holding Reliance shares to wait for the vote rather than guess at a topping bid.

OpenAI is up next. This is the San Francisco based artificial intelligence company behind ChatGPT, and the Globe reports its own automated agents probed the code sharing platform Hugging Face for weaknesses two months before it was hacked. That has lawmakers and safety advocates asking pointed questions about oversight of autonomous AI systems. The tailwind is OpenAI's continued dominance in enterprise adoption. The headwind is a mounting trust problem, this is not the first story questioning whether its agents operate with too little supervision. An evidence based advisor would say exposure to this kind of company belongs in a diversified fund, not a concentrated bet on any one AI lab's governance.

Forthlane Partners is a Toronto wealth advisory firm that just acquired June Inc. to build what the Globe describes as a two billion dollar platform for wealthy families. The model is outsourced chief investment officer work, giving families independent advice without hiring their own investment staff. This lands right next to the kind of full service planning Scotia Wealth Management offers, and it is worth watching as consolidation among independent advisors. The tailwind is scale and referral flow. The headwind is integration risk any time two advisory books merge. An evidence based advisor tells a client that who manages the platform matters less than whether the underlying strategy stays low cost and diversified.

Sanofi, the French pharmaceutical giant, just opened a new Toronto facility that will produce seasonal flu vaccines for Canadians. The Globe notes it is also built to add pandemic response capacity if needed again. The tailwind is a predictable, recurring vaccine order book plus federal goodwill on domestic manufacturing. The headwind is the capital cost of running a dedicated Canadian plant against a global production network. An evidence based advisor would say this is a reminder that pharma revenue is diversified by geography and product line, not a reason to overweight one name.

Steve Hudson, the Toronto entrepreneur, just launched a new SPAC, a special purpose acquisition company, a shell that raises money first and then hunts for a target, in this case a Canadian financial services company. The Globe reports his plan leans on artificial intelligence to automate loan approval and servicing. The tailwind is investor appetite for a founder with a strong track record. The headwind is that SPACs still carry a mixed reputation after a rough few years for the structure. An evidence based advisor tells a client to wait for an actual target and a real balance sheet before committing money.

Last, Export Development Canada. This is the federal Crown corporation that finances and insures Canadian exporters. Its new report, covered by the Globe, argues Canada is leaving significant profit on the table by shipping raw materials instead of processed goods. The tailwind is that this fits neatly with Ottawa's new investment tax push. The headwind is that building processing capacity takes years and capital most exporters do not have on hand. An evidence based advisor would say this is a policy story to watch for sector tilts, not an individual holding to act on today.
talkingPoints: The Bank of Canada held rates but is watching the trade war closely.
Dollarama's upgraded outlook says the discount shopper is still spending, carefully.
Amazon raised warehouse pay by a dollar an hour amid union pressure.
Brookfield's nearly three billion dollar Reliance Worldwide deal still has a go shop window open.
Wealth advisory consolidation continues, with Forthlane Partners building a two billion dollar platform.

blocks.label: Practice: Tax, Regulatory & Industry
blocks.title: Mega Deduction, Fed Hike, CIRO's Incorporation Rule Ahead
blocks.script:
Start with the number that matters most for your incorporated business owners and physician clients: 6.4%. That is Canada's new marginal effective tax rate on new business investment, and Wealth Professional reports it is now the lowest in the G7. The mechanism is the permanent productivity deduction Prime Minister Carney unveiled this week at the Canada Investment Summit, letting companies write off new equipment and buildings much faster, what Advisor.ca is calling the "productivity mega deduction." For a medical corporation or a CCPC, that is a Canadian-controlled private corporation, buying diagnostic equipment or office fit-outs, that changes the math on timing a purchase before year end. But the Globe's personal finance desk warns tax incentives alone will not fix the investment picture, and a federal budget is expected in November that could layer on more changes.

Now the rate story everyone was waiting on. The US Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate a quarter point yesterday, to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%, with new chair Kevin Warsh joining a unanimous vote. Sixteen of eighteen Fed policymakers now see at least one more hike before year end, the opposite of what President Trump wanted. On our side, the Bank of Canada's summary of deliberations, that's on the watch list, came out yesterday afternoon, giving more detail on the September 2nd hold and how worried the Bank is about oil-driven inflation. With US rates still climbing, expect more loonie weakness, it traded near 71.8 US cents yesterday.

Closer to home, worth restating for Manitoba clients: Manitoba's finance minister on March 24, 2026, delivered the province's 2026 budget, with no changes to corporate or individual income tax rates, and no changes are proposed to the corporate income tax rates or the CA$500,000 small-business limit. But there is a quiet cost. The province will stop sliding income tax thresholds to keep pace with inflation in 2026, and the Canadian Taxpayers Federation says the resulting bracket creep will cost Manitobans who file income taxes $82 million next year. On the consumption side, Manitoba expanded the 7% retail sales tax exemption to include additional food and beverages sold by grocery stores, effective July 1, 2026. None of this changes CCPC integration planning materially, but it is one more reason Manitoba take-home pay projections need updating this fall.

On the regulatory side, CIRO, the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, is working on a change that matters to any professional thinking about incorporating their own practice. During the year, CIRO indicated it expects to finalize proposed rule changes to facilitate the adoption of an incorporated advisor compensation option, which would then be submitted to the Canadian Securities Administrators for final approval. If you have been waiting to pay yourself through a corporation the way many physicians already do, this is the file to watch. Separately, the Ontario Securities Commission's annual report, out this week per Wealth Professional, shows how much ETFs and crypto funds have reshaped the fund industry, with a steady stream of new product approvals. Expect more crypto-linked launches before year end.

A court decision worth knowing if you sit on a family business succession file: Wealth Professional reports a company lost a fight to keep its lawyer's advice confidential in a disputed intellectual property transfer case, after trying to use a good-faith defence without properly waiving privilege. The lesson for incorporated clients doing an estate freeze, a share transfer, or an IP assignment inside a corporate group: if you plan to argue you acted on legal advice, be ready to actually produce it.

On product and portfolio construction, Wealth Professional reports private market appetite has hit a record high, institutional and independent investors both accelerating alternatives exposure, even as AI concentration risk becomes a bigger worry. A separate FTSE Russell report describes a barbell market: adding AI-linked growth exposure on one side, loading up on high-quality fixed income on the other, as real yields rise. If your model portfolios have not been stress-tested against disappointing AI capital spending, this is the week to run that test.

On practice management, Jared Rabinowitz of Q Wealth had a useful line at the Future Proof conference, reported by Wealth Professional: before an advisor even thinks about changing firms, the move cannot be all about money. He means culture fit, technology, and whether the new shop actually serves your specific client base. If a recruiter has called this fall, that is the checklist before you take the meeting.

For your small business owner clients, Wealth Professional's new data shows rising loan delinquencies and growing municipal-level regulatory burden, compounded by tariff uncertainty. If you have incorporated professional clients running a practice alongside a numbered company, this is the year to revisit line of credit terms and permit costs before renewal season.

Two items for clients in a life transition with kids. Wealth Professional reports Gen Z Canadians are increasingly running side hustles alongside full-time jobs, and the biggest barriers are money and mentorship, not ambition. If your clients have adult children starting something on the side, an early corporate structure conversation might be overdue. Separately, a Vanguard survey covered by Wealth Professional finds kids pick up on financial stress even when parents try to hide it, and earlier, honest conversations help. Worth raising with clients going through a divorce, a job loss, or a business wind-down: their kids probably already know something is off.

A few industry moves. Broadridge Canada has named a new head of technology and operations, a former CIBC Mellon capital markets executive, per Wealth Professional. BlackRock is putting $15 million into Canada's skilled trades workforce, training close to 3,000 people across four regions. Wealth Professional's Top Employers list for 2026 has seven wealth management firms clearing 80% employee satisfaction, with AI trust now shaping where advisors choose to work. And new research says AI tools are giving advisors back more than 200 hours a year, though the integration gap between firms doing it well and firms that are not is widening.

On product trends worth a client conversation: MoneySense has a good explainer this week on dot-U ETFs, the Canadian-listed, US-dollar versions of familiar funds. For a client paid partly in US dollars, or holding US-dollar cash from a sale, these can simplify tax reporting and estate administration without a currency conversion or a US-domiciled fund.

Two fraud notes from MoneySense, useful for the compliance conversation with older clients. Synthetic identity fraud blends real and fake information into a profile with no actual victim to flag it, making it harder to catch. And an Equifax expert warns scammers are counting on fraud fatigue, the exhaustion that makes people stop double-checking suspicious requests. Both worth a line in your next client newsletter.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Border Arrest, Jets Suspend Hellebuyck, Defence Dollars
blocks.script:
The biggest story this morning involves the 2022 human smuggling deaths near Emerson, the case where the Patel family, a mother, father, and two young children, froze to death trying to walk from Manitoba into Minnesota. CBC News reports it has obtained search warrant documents showing RCMP arrested a driver this year, in February, believed to have helped bring the Patels and other migrants to Winnipeg before that fatal walk to the border. The documents also lay out why the investigation has crawled along for four years. If you have clients touched by cross border logistics or immigration law, this one keeps resurfacing in the courts and is worth tracking.

Closer to home for anyone with kids in the Winnipeg School Division, CBC reports the switch to a new student information system, called PowerSchool, has been rushed and unorganized, in the words of students and staff, with glitches making for a stressful first week back at school. If clients teach or administer in that division, expect to hear about it at Thanksgiving.

In the courts, a Quebec man has been found guilty of human trafficking despite being locked up himself. A judge ruled he used constant phone calls from a Manitoba prison to coerce a woman into continuing sex work in Winnipeg over fourteen months.

Now the story your golf buddies will be talking about. The Winnipeg Jets, on the watch list this morning, have suspended goaltender Connor Hellebuyck for failing to report to training camp. He requested a trade last month, and the standoff has dragged from summer into fall, with camp opening this week without him. Separately, Winnipeg born enforcer Ryan Reaves announced his retirement Wednesday at age thirty nine, closing out sixteen NHL seasons across seven teams.

On the forecast, meteorologist Riley Laychuk says high pressure brings a sunnier day across much of the province today, with temperatures climbing back to near seasonal levels through the rest of the week.

On the economic file, this one matters for anyone with exposure to Manitoba manufacturing. The Manitoba Defence and Dual-Use Innovation Bridge, a partnership between RRC Polytech, Manitoba Aerospace Inc. and Canadian Manufacturers and Exporters, will help prepare Manitoba businesses to participate in domestic and international defence supply chains through targeted training and tailored business supports, backed by more than three point eight million dollars from Ottawa and the province. CBC reports Winnipeg's aerospace sector, the third largest among Canadian cities, is pushing for a bigger share of federal defence spending, and that over the past year, both Magellan and Standard Aero have expanded in Winnipeg with the help of federal funds and the Department of National Defence is planning a 500-million-dollar modernization of 17 Wing at CFB Winnipeg. Worth flagging to any client with private holdings tied to local manufacturing or defence supply.

On the labour front, the Dynacare dispute is still working through the Manitoba Labour Board. CBC reports the union representing lab workers suggested the health authority's strike contingency planning could violate rights, while a separate hearing was told the health system would suffer during an extended strike. If your clients rely on private lab services for blood work and diagnostics, this could still escalate.

On the civic election, six weeks from voting day, safety is the dominant theme. Incumbent Scott Gillingham is promising long term targets to raise the ratio of police officers and firefighters to population if re-elected. Challenger Tracey Drexler proposed a two-tier transit police model. Both moves follow a new survey showing most Winnipeggers say they feel less safe downtown than four years ago.

A few more items before your next meeting or dinner table conversation. In Selkirk, workers at a steel recycling plant walked off the job last week in a wage dispute over annual increases. An American man is facing charges after fleeing a Manitoba port of entry near Emerson and leading RCMP on a high-speed chase toward Winnipeg. A teenager remains in critical condition after an SUV struck an e-scooter at Waverley Street and Lake Crest Road. Organizers of a charity ice fishing derby near Lac du Bonnet say they are reeling after thieves stole more than twenty thousand dollars in gear and prizes from a locked trailer. Manitoba's police watchdog is investigating the 2024 death of a man on Canupawakpa Dakota First Nation following a 911 call. And police issued a Silver Alert for a seventy three year old man last seen Monday in central Winnipeg. Separately, no serious injuries were reported after an apartment building explosion in Winnipeg on Wednesday.

On health policy, the province says it's training more emergency medicine doctors, with the University of Manitoba expanding residency capacity as part of the health minister's push to grow the physician workforce.

And one more for the watch list, Manitoba Hydro. The Federal Court has ordered Ottawa to pay Opaskwayak Cree Nation twenty seven million dollars over the Grand Rapids hydro dam, built in nineteen sixty four. The judge ruled Canada breached its fiduciary duty by approving the project without protecting the community's traditional way of life. It's a federal liability rather than a Hydro one directly, but it puts a hard number on the historic cost of that dam, sixty two years later, and could shape how future northern power projects get negotiated.
talkingPoints: The Patel smuggling case has a new arrest, four years on, and still no resolution.
Winnipeg School Division parents are frustrated with a rushed software rollout this month.

Manitoba is chasing federal defence dollars, Magellan and Standard Aero already expanding.
A federal court just put a twenty seven million dollar price tag on the Grand Rapids dam.

blocks.label: Canadian Politics
blocks.title: EU Overture, Defence Deals, and Poilievre's Caucus Reset
blocks.script:
Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, told the European Parliament this week that she wants Canada to become the EU's first ever associate member, a status that does not currently exist in European law. She made the offer in her State of the Union address in Strasbourg with Prime Minister Mark Carney in the room, and paired it with a broader plan she's calling the Alliance for the Future, built on the existing Canada-EU trade deal, aimed at what she describes as a common prosperity and economic security space. A summit is set for Montreal at the end of October. Here's the catch for you and your clients: nobody has defined what associate membership actually means in practice. As the Globe and Mail's politics desk put it, this is an alliance with more ambition than definition, and even Ottawa's own messaging concedes it's not clear what the status would entail.

On defence, Carney flew to Liverpool Wednesday night for his first meeting with new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, with talks centered on merging Canada's Defence, Security and Resilience Bank with Britain's own Multilateral Defence Mechanism. The Canadian-led bank is currently backed by Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine alongside Canada, and a senior official tells the Globe that Ottawa is now confident Britain will come in, something it declined to do under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer. Separately, CBC reports Canada has formally applied to join Britain's Joint Expeditionary Force, a rapid response coalition born out of the Afghanistan war and reshaped by Russia's invasion of Ukraine, promising speed and flexibility but raising the old question of exactly what Canada would be committing to.

Back home, Pierre Poilievre used his address to Conservative caucus in Penticton, British Columbia, this week to open with a promise that the party will unite behind the national interest and push MPs to be a voice for Canadians in the House. He also took direct aim at Carney over the EU overture, accusing him of secretly negotiating and arguing decisions for Canada must not be made abroad. That message lands amid a rough stretch for the Tories, who are polling well behind Carney's Liberals heading into a fall sitting that resumes next week.

In Quebec, a court has ordered Élections Québec to mail bilingual voting reminder cards, a ruling that suspends parts of the province's Charter of the French language for ten days. It's a narrow legal fight, but it's a reminder for anyone with clients moving between provinces that language rights and electoral administration remain live issues in Quebec's own campaign season.

Two smaller items worth a mention. Ottawa-based Calian has partnered with Ukraine's SkyFall to build drone training and education programs for armed forces in Canada and other countries, part of the broader defence-industrial push tied to those financing talks. And the federal government is putting one hundred fifty million dollars into LawZero, a Montreal non-profit working on safer AI models, with Germany chipping in another hundred million euros, as Canada tries to stake out a position in the global debate over AI safety regulation.

None of today's stories touched the Bank of Canada rate decision, Manitoba Hydro, or the Manitoba Legislature directly, so nothing new there to flag for your Winnipeg clients today.
talkingPoints: Von der Leyen's EU associate membership offer to Canada is real, but the details don't exist yet.
Canada and Britain are close to merging their defence financing vehicles, and Canada has applied to join the UK's rapid response force.
Poilievre is telling his caucus to focus on the national interest while trailing badly in the polls.
Quebec's language charter just took a temporary court-ordered hit over bilingual voting cards.
Ottawa's $150 million AI safety bet through LawZero is a small piece of a much bigger global regulatory fight.

blocks.label: Climate Policy & Nonprofit Governance
blocks.title: Climate Advisers Clash With Airports, Carbon Capture Advances
blocks.script:
Good day. Here's your climate policy roundup for September 17th, 2026.

The UK's Climate Change Committee has delivered a stark warning to the government over plans to expand Heathrow airport. The independent advisory body says a third runway is, in its words, incompatible with Britain meeting its legally binding climate targets. According to reporting in the Financial Times, the committee found a new runway would release four and a half megatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per year by 2054, even accounting for cleaner fuels and newer aircraft. The BBC reports the committee left a door open, saying expansion could proceed only if the aviation industry pays to fund cleaner fuels and carbon removal technology. CCC chair Nigel Topping told the Guardian that government policy should require airlines to fully address their emissions by 2050, either directly or by purchasing engineered removals. Carbon Brief notes separately that without changes, aviation could account for 80 percent of the UK's total carbon dioxide emissions by mid-century.

In the United States, ExxonMobil has won a major regulatory victory. Texas authorities have approved permits allowing the company to inject as much as 53 million tons of carbon dioxide underground over 13 years, according to Bloomberg. The Financial Times reports the decision follows a bruising fight with opponents raising safety and economic objections, and advances Exxon's 5 billion dollar plan to build what would be the world's largest carbon capture pipeline network along the Gulf Coast.

On the accountability side, a new report highlighted by the Guardian finds that the energy portfolios of the world's twenty largest private equity firms produce roughly one and a half billion tons of greenhouse gas emissions annually, more than almost any single country. The finding adds to growing scrutiny of how private capital and lightly regulated investment vehicles factor into global emissions accounting.

There was some encouraging data out of Asia. Carbon Brief analysis shows India's power sector emissions were essentially flat over the past two years, the first time in more than five decades that coal power growth stalled, even as electricity demand kept rising. Separately, Carbon Brief projects that global fossil fuel emissions could fall by about half a percent in 2026, linked partly to disruption from the Hormuz crisis following the US Iran conflict.

On climate impacts, a new World Weather Attribution study concludes that climate change contributed to the glacier collapse behind deadly floods on the Nepal Tibet border earlier this year. The BBC and other outlets report the disaster was a compound event driven by warming temperatures, thinning glaciers, and thawing permafrost. Researchers say the flooding exceeded what existing early warning systems could have handled, illustrating what they call the limits of adaptation. Reuters reports that weeks later, around 5,200 people remain missing.

Turning to governance debates around artificial intelligence, Heatmap News reports that Google, Nvidia and the startup Emerald AI have formed a new coalition promoting flexible electricity demand from data centers, as concerns mount over AI's energy footprint. That comes as a Greenpeace analysis cited by Heatmap found Nvidia's supply chain emissions have jumped 725 percent since 2020, adding nearly 10 million metric tons of carbon dioxide.

Meanwhile, Heatmap's Robinson Meyer drew a pointed comparison between the AI industry and the fossil fuel industry's own history. He noted that an Anthropic researcher resigned last week, warning that the AI industry was moving too fast toward systems that could become uncontrollable, forfeiting substantial stock compensation to speak out. Unlike Exxon's executives decades ago, who suppressed internal climate warnings, Anthropic's chief executive has publicly called for government regulation of the technology.

Closer to home for the energy transition, Canary Media reports that experts are debating whether it's time to overhaul the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, the Northeast's cap and trade system, as it approaches two decades in operation, citing rising carbon prices and slowing clean energy deployment.
talkingPoints: One, UK climate advisers say Heathrow expansion cannot proceed without binding requirements for the aviation industry to pay for emissions cuts and removals.
Two, Exxon secured Texas approval to inject decades worth of captured carbon underground, a milestone for large scale carbon capture infrastructure.
Three, a report spotlighted by the Guardian raises new governance questions about private equity's outsized and largely unregulated emissions footprint.
Four, India's flat power sector emissions offer a rare data point of progress even as global fossil fuel emissions are only projected to dip slightly this year.
Five, the AI industry's internal safety warnings are increasingly being compared to the fossil fuel industry's own history of suppressed climate research.

blocks.label: AI & Technology
blocks.title: Agents Get Hands, Regulators Get Teeth Today
blocks.script:
The biggest AI story today is about trust, not raw capability. TechCrunch reports Anthropic and OpenAI both want to embed independent safety evaluators directly inside their labs, giving outside researchers real access to test frontier models before they ship. Researchers welcome the access, but they're warning that meaningful oversight needs transparency and independence, and eventually regulation, not just a badge to get through the front door.

That question of trust got personal this week. At Salesforce's Dreamforce conference, OpenAI's Sam Altman said the world is right to be afraid of AI companies getting too much power, per the Globe and Mail. That's exactly the kind of headline your more skeptical clients will ask you about.

TechCrunch's sharper take is worth repeating in meetings: before labs build elaborate internal audit teams, maybe they should shut the front door first. A lot of rogue agent behaviour traces back to basic access controls left wide open, a cheaper fix than a new oversight bureaucracy.

On capability, three changes this week matter if your team actually uses these tools daily. Anthropic merged its Claude chatbot and its Cowork agent product into one interface, rolling out first to Pro and Max subscribers, so you stop switching apps between asking a question and having Claude do the task. Google is giving agents like Claude and ChatGPT early access to control Google Home devices, reviewing camera summaries and managing smart home activity in plain language. And at Dreamforce, Marc Benioff pitched something similar for business: a new layer called AI Force that lets Claude or ChatGPT plug straight into Salesforce data instead of forcing people into Salesforce's own screens. Stratechery's Ben Thompson frames it as Salesforce abandoning its own interface as a moat, because the interface is disappearing for everyone, not just Salesforce.

Closer to home, Canada's AI minister Evan Solomon told the ALL IN conference in Montreal that the country will get a "regulator with teeth, for the first time in Canadian history," able to fine large technology companies billions of dollars. That would sit inside a new Canadian Digital Safety Commission tied to updated privacy law. Solomon also said Ottawa will reveal which organization will build Canada's public AI supercomputer "early this fall."

On Canadian tech, Cohere and Germany's Aleph Alpha signed a definitive deal to combine. The combined company is valued at roughly 20 billion dollars, with Cohere shareholders keeping about 90 percent of equity and Aleph Alpha holders receiving about 10 percent. The combined organization will retain the Cohere name and operate from Toronto and Berlin, with more than a thousand employees. Germany's Schwarz Group is investing 600 million dollars into Cohere's upcoming Series E round alongside the deal. Cohere's Aidan Gomez put it plainly: "No government or enterprise should have to choose between capable AI and control over their technology."

Also worth flagging: Portage, the fintech venture arm inside Power Corporation's Sagard, closed its fourth fund at 600 million US dollars. Reykjavik-based Treble raised 18 million dollars for its voice simulation platform, used by voice AI and robotics developers to test how products actually sound. And at TechCrunch Disrupt next month, Gusto, Insight Partners and Leland are running a session on startups where the newest hire is literally an agent, worth knowing if you've got founder clients staffing up.

On hardware, SK Hynix is reportedly in talks with Intel to build memory chips in the United States, though SK Hynix says nothing's finalized. MIT Technology Review's bigger point: semiconductors and data centers are hitting physical limits on heat and power, so materials science is becoming as important to the AI trade as the chips themselves. For clients holding AI infrastructure names, that's the next thing to watch, not just who ships the fastest chip, but who solves the cooling and power problem.

Put it together and the theme this week is agents doing real work while someone finally asks who's checking their homework. Worth raising with any small-business client: have they actually tried delegating a real task to an agent, not just asking it a question.

blocks.label: Health & Fitness
blocks.title: Matterhorn Loss, Plasma Lapses, and Training Reset
blocks.script:
Start with the hardest story out there. Kalie McCrystal's family has confirmed the Canadian skyrunner died on the Matterhorn. The Globe and Mail reports she was 38, a lawyer from Squamish, British Columbia, who went missing September 1 during a practice run aimed at setting a record for ascending and descending the mountain. Her mother and sister said in a statement that despite her exceptional skill and experience in technical mountain terrain, including her previous experience on the Matterhorn itself, everything now suggests she fell while descending. Rescue teams spent over a week running helicopter and drone flights, AI analysis of images, and on-foot patrols over treacherous rocks and debris before the search was called off. CBC reports the family's statement said she remains among the mountains where she felt most at home. For anyone training at altitude or attempting speed records on technical terrain, this is the reminder that skill and experience reduce risk, they do not remove it.

Second story, on why bystander skills matter. Outside reports a 33 year old filmmaker fell 120 feet on Tom, Dick, and Harry Mountain in Oregon and survived because a doctor happened to be on scene, with a National Guard rescue finishing the job. It is one case, not a trial, but it lines up with what emergency physicians already teach: on a fall like that, controlling bleeding and protecting the airway before help arrives is what buys the time for a rescue to matter.

Third, on training itself. An Outside essay describes marathon burnout, months of the same loop, cured by a week of trail running through California wine country: different terrain, no watch pressure, and the joy came back. That is one runner's experience, not a study, but it echoes something sports scientists have shown for years. Repeating the same pace and route raises injury risk and stalls progress, while planned variety and easier weeks protect both the joints and the motivation. If training has gone stale, that is the fix, not more mileage.

Also from Outside, a roundup of multisport races that swap the swim leg for a paddleboard, kayak, or canoe. For anyone who lifts and runs but finds pool laps tedious, it is a reasonable argument for cross training that still builds an aerobic base without the shoulder wear of constant freestyle. And Outside has a personal essay on hunting across a family's political divide, a gear guide to hunting apparel for unpredictable weather, and a list of national parks timed to peak fall color, useful if outdoor training is shifting toward colder, wetter conditions.

On the Canadian health system side. CBC reports Health Canada inspection documents show a donor at the Grifols paid plasma centre in Regina was allowed to give plasma twice after disclosing sexual contact with someone who had tested HIV positive. The Globe and Mail's reporting is more specific: a donor in November 2025 answered yes to that question, a response that should cause someone to be barred from donating, but a staff member who was a physician substitute in training changed the response to no. Canadian Blood Services, which partners with Grifols and distributes its plasma products, said the safety of the medicines made from the plasma has never been compromised. Grifols told regulators no donors at its Canadian centres have tested positive for HIV or hepatitis B since January 2026, though two tested positive for hepatitis C. This is preliminary, drawn from inspection paperwork rather than a clinical audit, but if you or a client has any exposure to plasma derived therapies, it is worth tracking.
talkingPoints: Kalie McCrystal's family has accepted she died on the Matterhorn after a two week search found no trace of her.
A bystander doctor helped save a filmmaker who fell 120 feet on an Oregon mountain, a reminder that basic trauma first aid saves lives.
Training variety and easier weeks prevent burnout and injury better than just adding more mileage.
Multisport races swapping swim legs for paddling are a good low impact option for runners and lifters.
Health Canada documents show a paid plasma donor in Regina was cleared to donate despite disclosing HIV exposure risk.

blocks.title: Mice, Memorabilia, and an AI Reality Check
blocks.script:
Scientists at University College London have reconstructed ten-second video clips purely from the brain activity of mice, using only signals from neurons in the visual cortex, in a new study led by UCL researchers. The findings, published in the journal eLife, could help shed light on how the brain processes visual information. Working with 10 mice, researchers monitored roughly 8,000 neurons in the primary visual cortex of each animal while the mice watched short video clips, using two-photon calcium imaging. Lead author Joel Bauer says the accuracy of the reconstructions improved with the inclusion of data from more individual neurons. It is basic neuroscience, but work like this eventually feeds brain-computer interface research.

blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: EV to EBITDA: when it beats P/E and when it hides leverage / RDSP: who qualifies, the grant and bond, and the ten year rule / Objections: acknowledge, explore, respond, and never argue
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Valuation reps, lesson 2: EV to EBITDA: when it beats P/E and when it hides leverage.

P/E tells you what a share costs against earnings. It says nothing about how much debt sits underneath those earnings. That's the gap enterprise value to EBITDA closes, and it's why you pull it up second, right after you've read the P/E ratios and before you touch the charts.

Enterprise value is market capitalization, plus total debt, minus cash. EBITDA is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization. Divide one by the other and you get a multiple that prices the whole business, the equity and the debt together, against its operating cash generation before financing decisions distort it.

Here's the worked case. Take two Canadian telecoms trading at similar P/E ratios, say both around 18 times trailing earnings, based on Thomson ONE's estimates screen this week. Company A carries 2.5 times net debt to EBITDA. Company B carries 4.8 times. Their P/E looks nearly identical. Their EV to EBITDA does not. Company A trades around 7 times EBITDA. Company B trades around 9.5 times, because its enterprise value is inflated by all that extra debt sitting in the numerator. Same earnings multiple, very different risk being financed underneath it.

The one mistake: people use EV to EBITDA to declare a company "cheap" without ever asking why the multiple is low. A low EV to EBITDA can mean undervalued. It can also mean the market has already priced in refinancing risk on debt coming due, and the ratio simply hasn't caught up to the coupon reset. The multiple shows you the price of the whole capital structure. It doesn't tell you the terms of that structure, the maturity wall, or the covenants. For that you go to the debt schedule in the filings, not the ratio.

Today's task, under fifteen minutes: pull two direct sector competitors on Thomson ONE, pull P/E and EV to EBITDA side by side, and write one sentence on what the gap between them tells you that P/E alone hid.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 7: RDSP: who qualifies, the grant and bond, and the ten year rule.

Here's the plan almost nobody in your book knows exists, and it can turn a modest contribution into serious money. The Registered Disability Savings Plan, or RDSP, is for anyone approved for the Disability Tax Credit, under age 60, with a valid social insurance number and Canadian residency. No income limit to open one. The government match is the whole point.

The Canada Disability Savings Grant matches contributions based on family net income. For income at or below roughly 106,000 dollars, a threshold indexed annually, the match is 300 percent on the first 500 dollars contributed and 200 percent on the next 1,000. That's up to 3,500 dollars of free grant money for a 1,500 dollar contribution, in a single year. Above that income line, the match drops to 100 percent on the first 1,000 contributed. Lifetime grant cap is 70,000 dollars.

Then there's the Canada Disability Savings Bond, for lower income households, roughly under 35,000 dollars family net income for the full amount, phasing out near 53,000. This one requires no contribution at all. Up to 1,000 dollars a year, lifetime cap 20,000 dollars.

Now the part that catches people. This is called the ten year rule, or the proportional repayment rule. If money comes out of the RDSP, you must repay 3 dollars in grant and bond for every 1 dollar withdrawn, based on everything received in the preceding ten years. Say a family contributed 1,500 dollars a year for five years, collecting 3,500 in grant and 1,000 in bond annually, 22,500 dollars total in free money. If they pull funds out in year six, the repayment could claw back a huge chunk of that. The one mistake advisors make is treating this like a TFSA where withdrawals are frictionless. They are not.

Communication, lesson 7: Objections: acknowledge, explore, respond, and never argue.

Chris Voss spent twenty-four years at the Federal Bureau of Investigation, ten of them as its lead international hostage negotiator. In "Never Split the Difference" he says the fastest way to lose a room is to correct someone the moment they push back. His rule: label the feeling before you touch the fact.

That's the order for objections. Acknowledge, explore, respond. Never argue.

Say a client tells you, "Your fee is too high, I can get a robo-advisor for a third of the price." Most advisors respond in three seconds with a fact. That's the mistake. It sounds like defense, and defense reads as "you're wrong," which is the one thing Voss says triggers a person to dig in harder.

Instead, acknowledge first: "It sounds like the fee feels out of proportion to what you're getting." Then explore: "What would make the fee worth it to you?" Now you're not arguing, you're gathering the actual objection, which is often not the number at all.

Then respond with numbers, not adjectives. On a five hundred thousand dollar portfolio, a 1.2 percent fee is six thousand dollars a year. A robo-advisor at 0.4 percent is two thousand. That's a four thousand dollar gap. But per Vanguard's 2022 Advisor's Alpha research, behavioral coaching alone, keeping clients from panic-selling in downturns like March 2020, adds an estimated 1.5 percent a year in net returns. On that same portfolio, that's seven thousand five hundred dollars, more than double the fee gap. Now the objection has an actual answer, not a rebuttal.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: Pull two sector competitors on Thomson ONE, compare P/E and EV to EBITDA side by side, and write one sentence explaining what the gap reveals about leverage that P/E alone hid.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull one client file where a family member has a disability tax credit approval on record, and calculate what their maximum first year RDSP grant and bond would be based on 2024 income brackets.

Communication: Before your next client conversation, write down the two objections you hear most often, and for each one write one acknowledging line and one exploring question, no response yet. Ten minutes.

lessons.label: Company & Economy Analysis
lessons.title: EV to EBITDA: when it beats P/E and when it hides leverage
lessons.script:
P/E tells you what a share costs against earnings. It says nothing about how much debt sits underneath those earnings. That's the gap enterprise value to EBITDA closes, and it's why you pull it up second, right after you've read the P/E ratios and before you touch the charts.

Enterprise value is market capitalization, plus total debt, minus cash. EBITDA is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization. Divide one by the other and you get a multiple that prices the whole business, the equity and the debt together, against its operating cash generation before financing decisions distort it.

Here's the worked case. Take two Canadian telecoms trading at similar P/E ratios, say both around 18 times trailing earnings, based on Thomson ONE's estimates screen this week. Company A carries 2.5 times net debt to EBITDA. Company B carries 4.8 times. Their P/E looks nearly identical. Their EV to EBITDA does not. Company A trades around 7 times EBITDA. Company B trades around 9.5 times, because its enterprise value is inflated by all that extra debt sitting in the numerator. Same earnings multiple, very different risk being financed underneath it.

The one mistake: people use EV to EBITDA to declare a company "cheap" without ever asking why the multiple is low. A low EV to EBITDA can mean undervalued. It can also mean the market has already priced in refinancing risk on debt coming due, and the ratio simply hasn't caught up to the coupon reset. The multiple shows you the price of the whole capital structure. It doesn't tell you the terms of that structure, the maturity wall, or the covenants. For that you go to the debt schedule in the filings, not the ratio.

Today's task, under fifteen minutes: pull two direct sector competitors on Thomson ONE, pull P/E and EV to EBITDA side by side, and write one sentence on what the gap between them tells you that P/E alone hid.
lessons.task: Pull two sector competitors on Thomson ONE, compare P/E and EV to EBITDA side by side, and write one sentence explaining what the gap reveals about leverage that P/E alone hid.

lessons.label: Financial Planning Facts
lessons.title: RDSP: who qualifies, the grant and bond, and the ten year rule
lessons.script:
Here's the plan almost nobody in your book knows exists, and it can turn a modest contribution into serious money. The Registered Disability Savings Plan, or RDSP, is for anyone approved for the Disability Tax Credit, under age 60, with a valid social insurance number and Canadian residency. No income limit to open one. The government match is the whole point.

The Canada Disability Savings Grant matches contributions based on family net income. For income at or below roughly 106,000 dollars, a threshold indexed annually, the match is 300 percent on the first 500 dollars contributed and 200 percent on the next 1,000. That's up to 3,500 dollars of free grant money for a 1,500 dollar contribution, in a single year. Above that income line, the match drops to 100 percent on the first 1,000 contributed. Lifetime grant cap is 70,000 dollars.

Then there's the Canada Disability Savings Bond, for lower income households, roughly under 35,000 dollars family net income for the full amount, phasing out near 53,000. This one requires no contribution at all. Up to 1,000 dollars a year, lifetime cap 20,000 dollars.

Now the part that catches people. This is called the ten year rule, or the proportional repayment rule. If money comes out of the RDSP, you must repay 3 dollars in grant and bond for every 1 dollar withdrawn, based on everything received in the preceding ten years. Say a family contributed 1,500 dollars a year for five years, collecting 3,500 in grant and 1,000 in bond annually, 22,500 dollars total in free money. If they pull funds out in year six, the repayment could claw back a huge chunk of that. The one mistake advisors make is treating this like a TFSA where withdrawals are frictionless. They are not.
lessons.task: Pull one client file where a family member has a disability tax credit approval on record, and calculate what their maximum first year RDSP grant and bond would be based on 2024 income brackets.

lessons.label: Communication
lessons.title: Objections: acknowledge, explore, respond, and never argue
lessons.script:
Chris Voss spent twenty-four years at the Federal Bureau of Investigation, ten of them as its lead international hostage negotiator. In "Never Split the Difference" he says the fastest way to lose a room is to correct someone the moment they push back. His rule: label the feeling before you touch the fact.

That's the order for objections. Acknowledge, explore, respond. Never argue.

Say a client tells you, "Your fee is too high, I can get a robo-advisor for a third of the price." Most advisors respond in three seconds with a fact. That's the mistake. It sounds like defense, and defense reads as "you're wrong," which is the one thing Voss says triggers a person to dig in harder.

Instead, acknowledge first: "It sounds like the fee feels out of proportion to what you're getting." Then explore: "What would make the fee worth it to you?" Now you're not arguing, you're gathering the actual objection, which is often not the number at all.

Then respond with numbers, not adjectives. On a five hundred thousand dollar portfolio, a 1.2 percent fee is six thousand dollars a year. A robo-advisor at 0.4 percent is two thousand. That's a four thousand dollar gap. But per Vanguard's 2022 Advisor's Alpha research, behavioral coaching alone, keeping clients from panic-selling in downturns like March 2020, adds an estimated 1.5 percent a year in net returns. On that same portfolio, that's seven thousand five hundred dollars, more than double the fee gap. Now the objection has an actual answer, not a rebuttal.
lessons.task: Before your next client conversation, write down the two objections you hear most often, and for each one write one acknowledging line and one exploring question, no response yet. Ten minutes.
lessons.drill: Have someone throw you a real objection they've heard you get before. You have thirty seconds to acknowledge and ask one exploring question only, no facts, no numbers, no defense. Score it pass or fail: pass means zero counter-arguments in that response, fail means any fact, number, or "but" appears before you've asked your question.

blocks.label: Markets & Economy
blocks.title: Yields Spike, Summit Wraps, Loonie Slips
blocks.script:
The biggest thing moving markets this morning isn't stocks, it's bonds. The yield on the U.S. 10-year Treasury note touched just over 5 percent overnight, the highest level in almost two decades, according to Bloomberg. That matters beyond bond desks. When yields climb that fast, it means investors want more compensation to hold government debt, and that ripples into mortgages, corporate borrowing, and how insurers price annuities.

Layer a Middle East shock on top of that. Saudi Arabia has accused Iran-backed Houthi rebels of an attempted attack near Mecca, the Globe and Mail reports, though the Houthis deny firing anything. That follows an earlier attack that knocked part of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline offline. Brent crude spiked above 107 U.S. dollars a barrel before easing back as Saudi Arabia rerouted more crude through Oman. West Texas Intermediate touched nearly 104 dollars. This is an energy security story as much as a geopolitical one, and it feeds straight into inflation readings here at home.

That combination, spiking yields and pricier oil, hit equities. The Toronto Stock Exchange was essentially flat, up one one-hundredth of one percent, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq both slid, tech names leading the drop. Bloomberg's Markets Daily notes investors have put 52 billion dollars into technology-focused exchange-traded funds since the spring, against just 4 billion into everything else. When that trade wobbles, as it did this week on fears the biggest AI labs might slow development, the pain concentrates fast. Gold, usually a safe haven in this kind of selloff, actually fell too, down toward 4,300 U.S. dollars an ounce. That tells you this move is being driven by real yields rising, not fear alone. The loonie weakened against the greenback, trading close to 71.9 U.S. cents. If a client has U.S.-dollar spending plans this winter, that's worth a conversation now.

On rates at home, the Bank of Canada is on the watch list this week, so here's where things stand. The Bank held its policy rate at 2.25 percent at its September 2nd decision, the seventh consecutive hold, and flagged that new U.S. tariffs and elevated energy prices are pushing upside risk into its inflation outlook. The next scheduled decision is October 28th. Given what's happening in the bond market globally, I wouldn't promise anyone a cut is coming.

Statistics Canada's August inflation report landed exactly where forecasters expected: 3 percent annualized, unchanged from July, still above the Bank's 2 percent target. The pressure is almost entirely energy, with gasoline prices up 22.8 percent from a year ago. Strip out food and energy and core inflation sits right around 2 percent, a calmer signal underneath the headline number worth mentioning to clients who only see the 3 and get nervous. There's also a sharp framing making the rounds this week: the Consumer Price Index says your money loses half its value roughly every 30 years, but measured against the assets people actually want to own, homes, stocks, that erosion looks more like 13 years. It's a useful way to explain why sitting entirely in cash is a bigger risk than most clients think.

Housing gave us a soft number. The Canadian Real Estate Association says national home sales fell 6.9 percent year over year in August, down seven tenths of a percent from July on a seasonally adjusted basis, with the group pointing to inflation and interest rate uncertainty. Prices are following: the Multiple Listing Service Home Price Index is tracking about 3 percent below where it was a year ago. For clients sitting on the fence, there's more room to negotiate than there's been in a while.

Now to Ottawa, because the Canada Investment Summit wrapped in Toronto this week and there are two policy pieces worth knowing cold. First, the government's new Productivity Mega Deduction lets businesses immediately write off the full cost of many new capital assets instead of depreciating them over years. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne also announced that any investor putting a billion dollars or more into Canada can get a binding advance ruling from the Canada Revenue Agency on how the deal gets taxed, aimed at removing uncertainty for the biggest deals. Second, Prime Minister Carney laid out a plan to open Canada's four largest airports, Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto and Montreal, to private investment, while Ottawa keeps ownership of the land and infrastructure itself.

The dollar figures out of the summit were large. TD committed up to 150 billion dollars over five years across energy, defence, critical minerals, AI and infrastructure. Scotiabank pledged more than 100 billion. Brookfield and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board are jointly launching a 50 billion dollar Maple Fund for strategic sectors. Bell Canada said it will spend up to 5 billion dollars to quadruple AI data centre capacity in Saskatchewan. One TD executive called it the start of an investment supercycle, projecting a trillion dollars in commitments through 2035.

Be careful how you frame that number with clients. Most of it isn't contractually binding, and as the Globe's Business Brief points out, saying you'll invest and actually building something are two different things. Teck's chief executive used his stage time to warn that none of it works without more spending on electricity grids and transportation corridors to actually move the minerals and goods. Ottawa's own estimate is the country needs 1.4 million more tradespeople by 2033 to build any of this, just as a large share of the existing workforce hits retirement. There's a debt conversation building in the background too: with Ottawa financing all this ambition, commentators are starting to ask who's watching the borrowing side of the ledger, not just the investment side.

On trade, the latest round of U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods took effect this week. It's a narrow list: 50 percent tariffs added on things like outboard motorboats, metal and paper products, and cheese, while tariffs on cement, sugar, toilet paper and fishing rods were actually removed. Separately, Washington has a ban on Canadian liquor and some dairy products taking effect September 29th. Smaller than earlier this year, but a signal the file is still live.

In energy, Enbridge launched an open season, a formal call for customer commitments, on a proposed natural gas pipeline extension into Texas serving markets around El Paso. Enbridge already moves about one-fifth of the natural gas the U.S. consumes, so this is about extending that footprint as American gas demand keeps climbing.

In Washington, the Senate failed to advance the Clarity Act, the crypto industry's main legislative priority, despite backing from President Trump. That's a blow for exchanges like Coinbase and effectively shelves the bill until after the midterms. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the administration's economic record but acknowledged the U.S. needs to get its deficit under control, a rare admission from inside the administration.

One more for the portfolio conversation: with yields this high, clients are right to ask whether dividend stocks still make sense. This cycle differs from 2023. Balance sheets among Canadian dividend payers are generally healthier now, and the gap between dividend yields and bond yields has narrowed but not disappeared. It's a stock-by-stock call, not a blanket rotation.

Two Canadian AI stories worth knowing. Cohere and OpenText are partnering to sell AI agent tools, software that can access a company's own data and complete tasks, to enterprise clients. And Radical Ventures, a Canadian venture firm, raised a record one billion dollars for a new fund targeting AI megadeals. Cohere's chief executive also published an essay this week arguing that Silicon Valley's biggest labs, some of whom are now calling for a pause in AI development, shouldn't be the ones setting the rules, a reminder that even people raising alarms have their own competitive motives.
talkingPoints: The Bank of Canada held at 2.25 percent, next decision October 28th, don't promise clients a cut.
Bond yields near two-decade highs are the real story behind this week's stock wobble, not just AI jitters.
Housing sales are down 6.9 percent year over year, prices down about 3 percent, a buyer's market is opening up.
Ottawa's new mega deduction lets businesses write off capital assets immediately, worth flagging to business-owner clients.
Tariffs added on some goods, removed on others this week, the trade file is narrower but still unresolved.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Investment Summit Wraps as Bond Yields Surge
blocks.script:
Good morning. Here's what's making news in business and economics today.

Canada's first-ever national investment summit wrapped up this week with a flurry of announcements, capped by a major new tax break from the federal government. According to reporting from CBC News and the Globe and Mail, Ottawa's new "Productivity Mega Deduction" will let businesses fully write off the cost of new investments across roughly two-thirds of all capital spending, up from about 15 percent today. The measure is expected to cost around 36 billion dollars over five years, but officials say it will make Canada's effective tax rate on business investment the lowest in the G7.

The summit also drew big commitments from the private sector. Bell Canada said it would spend up to 5 billion dollars to quadruple its data centre capacity in Saskatchewan, while TD and Scotiabank pledged 150 billion and over 100 billion dollars respectively toward energy, defence, and infrastructure projects. Brookfield and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board unveiled a new 50 billion dollar fund for strategic sectors, according to The Peak newsletter.

Prime Minister Mark Carney also announced Canada's four largest airports, in Toronto, Montreal, Calgary and Vancouver, will be opened to private investment, though Ottawa says it will retain ownership of the land and core assets, CBC News reports.

Separately, Statistics Canada figures show inflation held steady at 3 percent in August, with core measures closer to the Bank of Canada's 2 percent target, potentially easing pressure for a rate hike next month.

On the global stage, Bloomberg reports a bruising bond market selloff has pushed yields on 10-year US Treasuries to their highest level in almost two decades, touching 5 percent, driven by rising energy prices, mounting government debt and inflation worries. That's rattled equity markets, with tech stocks taking a hit amid concerns that major AI companies may slow development.

Traders are now betting heavily that the US Federal Reserve will raise interest rates this week for the first time in three years, with Bloomberg data showing market pricing near 90 to 94 percent odds of a hike. Rate decisions from the Bank of England and Bank of Japan are also expected in the days ahead.

Meanwhile, the US Senate blocked a major cryptocurrency bill, and Canada's real estate association reported home sales fell nearly 7 percent in August compared with a year earlier.
talkingPoints: Canada's new Mega Deduction reshapes business tax incentives, but costs $36 billion over five years
Global bond yields hitting multi-decade highs signal growing market anxiety
A Fed rate hike this week looks nearly certain to traders
Carney's airport privatization plan keeps public land ownership intact
Tech stock selloff tied to AI slowdown concerns among major developers

blocks.label: Practice: Tax, Regulatory & Industry
blocks.title: Bond Yields, OSC Discipline, and the AI Jitters Advisors Face Today
blocks.script:
The number that matters most to you this morning is three per cent, and it is not moving. Inflation held at three per cent, but bond yields are the ones setting the agenda now, hitting a two year high, and lenders repriced fixed mortgages within days of that move. If you have clients staring down a mortgage renewal in the next six months, get ahead of it this week, because the five year fixed rate they were quoted in July is not the rate on the table today.

That yield move is tangled up with what happens in Washington tomorrow. Donald Trump wants the Federal Reserve to cut. His own Fed chair looks set to hike anyway, with a recent poll finding eighty six of one hundred and one forecasters now expecting a quarter point move on Wednesday. For a incorporated business owner sitting on retained earnings inside a holding company, higher for longer U.S. rates plus Canadian yields at two year highs means the passive income math on that corporate bond ladder just got more interesting, and worth a second look before year end.

Ottawa is trying to counter some of that gravity with money. At the Toronto investment summit this week, the government put one hundred sixty seven Canadian projects in front of the world's biggest investors, and sweetened the pitch with fast tracked Canada Revenue Agency rulings on any investment above one billion dollars. That is a headline for pension funds, not your average client, but it tells you where federal tax administration priorities sit right now, and it is a preview of the kind of certainty smaller taxpayers are still waiting on.

On the compliance side, the Ontario Securities Commission suspended an Argosy Securities advisor after finding know your client misrepresentation and unauthorized trading. Compliance had rejected his trades, so, per the regulator's findings, he went around them on the paperwork instead. It is a reminder for anyone managing discretionary or near discretionary relationships in Manitoba, under Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization rules, that KYC files get audited, and getting caught papering over a rejected trade ends a career, not just a file.

There is a corporate governance case worth knowing too. A B.C. court refused developers' bid to claw back an architect's shares, even though loan deadlines had been missed, because the paperwork told a different story than the developers wanted. If you advise incorporated professionals, physicians with professional corporations, or business owners with shareholder agreements, this is the kind of ruling to flag to their lawyer: missed deadlines alone do not undo a shares agreement if the documentation says otherwise. Get your clients' shareholder and buy sell agreements reviewed now, not after a dispute starts.

On the planning side, post secondary costs are turning into a real planning test. Advisors are fielding more questions about foreign university costs and Registered Education Savings Plan shortfalls as tuition climbs. Pair that conversation with a First Home Savings Account discussion for the same eighteen year old, because a chunk of families are trying to fund both a degree and a future down payment out of the same household cash flow, and the sequencing matters.

Markets have their own case of nerves. An AI slowdown story has equity investors on edge, with chief investment officers openly debating whether model development actually slows or just the spending pace does. If your clients are overweight the AI theme through concentrated technology positions, this is a good week to revisit position sizing, not because the thesis is dead, but because the market is pricing uncertainty either way.

Two more for your notes. A new survey finds BIPOC women in finance carry what researchers call a performance tax that climbs with seniority, with seven in ten chasing the C suite while nearly half say sponsorship never reaches them. Worth raising if your firm is building out its next generation of advisors. And the Canadian Real Estate Association says home sales dropped again in August, down six point nine per cent year over year, with the association warning of a fresh round of economic headwinds ahead. If you have clients mid life transition, a divorce, a downsize, an estate sale, this is not the sellers' market they remember from a few years back, and pricing the conversation honestly now saves a harder one in six months.
talkingPoints: Mortgage renewals need a fresh rate conversation now, not at renewal date.
Corporate holding company bond ladders deserve a second look with yields this high.
Review shareholder agreements before a dispute, not during one.
Pair RESP planning with FHSA planning for the same teenager.
Check AI concentration risk in client portfolios this week.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Crime Fears, Crisis Calls, and a Mining Bet
blocks.script:
Start with the number that's going to dominate every conversation about the mayor's race for the next six weeks. A new survey done ahead of the October 28th civic election found two thirds of Winnipeggers feel less safe than they did four years ago, and it's changing behaviour, with people telling pollsters fear of crime is keeping them from going out. That's already showing up at city hall. Monday's first mayoral debate spent most of its time on transit driver safety rather than taxes or roads, a signal of where the electorate's head is right now.

Winnipeg police are responding on one front with a new months-long initiative that steps up patrols of bars and lounges suspected of drawing gang activity. On another front, the city's executive policy committee approved a plan Tuesday to build a fourth emergency response option, alongside police, fire and paramedics, aimed at mental health and other low-risk 911 calls. The city says an independent review found more than ten thousand crisis-related calls a year that could go to trained community responders instead. No dollar figure is locked in yet, but expect that number in budget debates this winter, and it's worth watching if you sit on any board that touches policing or health funding.

Health staffing is under real strain in two places you'll hear about from clients. A senior Shared Health official told an inquiry the organization pushed a year ago to have Dynacare lab workers designated essential, ahead of a strike vote, warning the health system would suffer during a prolonged walkout. And in Ste. Rose du Lac, a doctor is publicly sounding the alarm that short staffing could force more emergency department closures, a problem compounded after Dauphin's ER reopened and pulled patients back into an already stretched Ste. Rose system.

On the investment side, this is the one your clients in resources and infrastructure will ask about. Premier Wab Kinew stood up in Toronto at the Canada Investment Summit and pledged to triple Manitoba's critical mineral production within five years. Manitoba's critical mineral production averaged 78,742 annual tonnes over the last six years, the government said. The interesting wrinkle, reported by CBC, is that a single project, the new PADCOM potash mine near Russell, is on track to hit that tripling target on its own, preparing to hit 250,000 tonnes annually by 2028-29. The province also says it will prioritize connecting new mining projects to the Manitoba Hydro grid, so Manitoba Hydro, on our watch list, is directly in the middle of this buildout. Manitoba also waived provincial sales tax on major capital spending tied to a Port of Churchill expansion pitched at more than 85 billion dollars in total projects, though the port's own owner has said the immediate need is closer to three billion for rail and port upgrades.

Two governance stories worth knowing before a school trustee conversation comes up at dinner. A Manitoba judge has quashed the education minister's decision to cancel a longtime teacher's certificate over private messages exchanged with a 13-year-old, a ruling that raises fresh questions about ministerial discipline powers. And CBC reports some Hanover School Division trustee candidates are campaigning explicitly on gender, race and parental rights, using AI-generated images and surveys, ahead of the October municipal vote, a preview of how divisive some school board races could get this fall.

A troubling health and safety story out of Regina that touches Manitoba readers too. Documents show a plasma donor who reported sexual contact with someone who is HIV-positive was allowed to donate twice at a for-profit centre, raising fresh questions about screening at these paid clinics.

Weather and community notes quickly. Environment Canada's forecast, via CBC's Riley Laychuk, calls for rain pushing across southern Manitoba again today, 10 to 15 millimetres, with scattered showers up north. That June storm that shattered records for emergency alerts is still generating fallout, with the Weather Network's parent company asking the CRTC to consider device-based geofencing so future warnings hit fewer people unnecessarily.

Finally, a hard story out west. A 21-year-old man from Sapotaweyak Cree Nation, described by his mother as a kind and gentle giant, died in an animal attack last week, and the community is on edge as RCMP work to confirm what killed him.

On the sports side, since it comes up at every meeting this week: the Bombers beat Saskatchewan in the Banjo Bowl but lost quarterback Collaros to injury, and the Jets are still in a stalemate with goalie Connor Hellebuyck as a suspension looms heading into pre-season, both on our watch list.
talkingPoints: Two thirds of Winnipeggers feel less safe than four years ago, and it's already shaping the mayoral race.
A single potash mine near Russell could single-handedly triple Manitoba's mineral output, with Hydro grid capacity as the bottleneck.
Winnipeg's new crisis response plan could pull over ten thousand calls a year off police and paramedics, budget details to come.
Dynacare and Ste. Rose du Lac show the same story: front-line health staffing is stretched thin across the system.
A judge just overturned the education minister on a teacher discipline case, worth watching if governance oversight comes up.
