lessons.script:
The Registered Education Savings Plan, or RESP, is the only account where the government hands you free money just for contributing. That's the Canada Education Savings Grant, the CESG. For 2026, the rule is 20 percent on the first 2,500 dollars you contribute per beneficiary per year, so a maximum grant of 500 dollars a year. Lifetime CESG per child caps at 7,200 dollars. Lifetime contribution room per child is 50,000 dollars, no annual cap on contributions, just no extra grant past that 2,500 dollar sweet spot. Manitoba has no provincial top-up here, unlike Quebec's QESI. What you get in Manitoba is the federal CESG plus, for lower income families, the Canada Learning Bond, up to 2,000 dollars, paid with no contribution required at all.

Here's the withdrawal side, and this is where advisors earn their fee. Money coming out for school splits into two buckets. Post-Secondary Education withdrawals, PSE, are just your original contributions back, no tax, ever. Educational Assistance Payments, EAP, are the grant money plus all the growth, and that's taxed in the student's hands. Budget 2023 raised the EAP cap for the first 13 weeks of enrollment to 8,000 dollars for full-time students, up from 5,000. After those 13 weeks, no cap.

Worked example. A student starts university in September 2026. The RESP holds 40,000 dollars: 28,000 in contributions, 12,000 in grant and growth. Withdraw 8,000 dollars as EAP in year one. The student has little or no other income, so that 8,000 lands mostly or entirely under the basic personal amount and gets taxed at close to zero.

The mistake: families draw PSE first because it feels safer, "it's just my own money." That leaves the taxable EAP piling up for later years, when the student might be working part-time and actually paying tax on it, or worse, the program ends early and unused grant money has to be repaid to the government.

Your task today, ten minutes: pull one client's RESP statement, split the balance into contribution room used versus grant and growth, and write down which bucket you'd draw from first if withdrawals started this year.

lessons.label: Communication
lessons.title: Numbers people can hear: translating figures into comparisons and consequences
lessons.script:
You're in a board meeting. The finance chair says, "revenue grew 40 percent this year." Everyone nods. Nobody feels anything, because 40 percent of what.

That's the whole lesson: a number without a comparison is just a sound. A number with a comparison becomes a fact people can carry out of the room.

Chip Heath, the Stanford professor who wrote "Made to Stick" with his brother Dan, studied why some numbers stick and others vanish. The answer isn't precision, it's scale the listener already understands.

Worked example. A food bank tells its board, "we distributed 1.4 million pounds of food last year." True, but it slides past you. Reframe it: 1.4 million pounds is roughly 1,150,000 meals, or about 3,150 meals every single day the doors were open, or one meal every 27 seconds. Now the board member pictures a person eating, not a spreadsheet cell.

Same move works with money. The Chronicle of Philanthropy reported total US charitable giving hit 557 billion dollars in 2023. Say instead: that's roughly 1,700 dollars given, on average, for every person in the country, whether they gave a cent or not. That comparison makes a huge, abstract number personal.

The mistake almost everyone makes: leading with the percentage and skipping the base number. "We grew 40 percent" tells you nothing about size. Going from 10 clients to 14 is 40 percent. Going from 10,000 to 14,000 is also 40 percent. Always give the base, then the change, then what it means for the person in front of you.
lessons.task: Pull one statistic you use often, a client win, a board metric, a LinkedIn claim. Rewrite it three ways: as a rate per day or per person, as a comparison to something the listener already knows the size of, and as a consequence for one real person.
lessons.drill: Record yourself saying the original stat cold, ten seconds. Then record your rewritten version. Play both, unlabeled, to one other person. Ask them to repeat back what they remember thirty seconds later. Pass: they repeat the translated version accurately. Fail: they repeat the raw number, the wrong number, or nothing at all.

blocks.label: Markets & Economy
blocks.title: Oil Shock, Rate Bets, and Carney's Investment Push
blocks.script:
Start with oil, because it touches almost everything else you'll talk about with clients this week. Saudi Arabia has shut down its East-West pipeline after drone attacks over the weekend, and that route carries about seven million barrels a day across the kingdom to Red Sea ports, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz entirely. Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said it suspended operations on the pipeline as a precaution after multiple attacks, and the pipeline is critical in linking oil production sites in the Eastern Province with Yanbu on the kingdom's western coast, with full pumping capacity of about seven million barrels per day. Brent crude touched 108 US dollars a barrel this morning before easing back, and West Texas Intermediate is trading around 103. Brent crude rose as high as 108, while U.S. crude oil touched 103 per barrel. Layer on top of that a postponed diplomatic meeting between Iran and Gulf states over the Strait of Hormuz, and reports that Saudi export stocks at one port could run dry within five to seven days, and you've got a genuine supply scare, not just headline noise. Tell clients this matters for two reasons: pump prices, and inflation readings that feed straight into central bank decisions.

Which brings you to today's number. Statistics Canada releases the August Consumer Price Index this morning, and the Street is watching closely. A poll of economists expects the annual rate of inflation was three per cent last month, holding steady from July. Economists expect the headline CPI to remain unchanged at 3 per cent year over year, with the Bank of Canada's core measure forecast to rise by just 0.1 per cent. The story underneath the headline is energy. RBC economists say Canada has seen inflationary pressure coming mainly from higher energy prices, which are up around 23 per cent from a year ago, though there was slight relief at the pumps last month compared with earlier this summer. Grocery inflation has also been running hotter than the headline number for about a year and a half, so lower income households are still feeling squeezed even as the topline print looks tame.

On the Bank of Canada, and this one's on your watch list, the bank held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent at its September 2nd meeting. The August inflation figures come after the Bank of Canada left its key policy rate unchanged at 2.25 per cent earlier this month, and the central bank has held its policy rate steady in seven consecutive decisions as it tries to balance volatile global energy prices and U.S. tariffs hampering the economy. The next scheduled decision is October 28th, and most economists still expect another hold, but Governor Tiff Macklem has flagged that if rising energy costs start spilling into the price of other goods and services, a hike becomes live. Wednesday brings the bank's summary of deliberations, which should give you a clearer read on how seriously they're weighing the trade war and the Middle East conflict together. If a client asks you point blank whether the BoC is done cutting, the honest answer is that the bar for a move either way just got higher, and the risk has tilted toward a hike in early 2027 rather than a cut.

South of the border, this is shaping up as a pivotal week for central banks generally. The Federal Reserve decides Wednesday, followed by the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan on successive days. Markets have swung toward pricing in a Fed hike, not a cut, after a hotter than expected core inflation print Friday. JPMorgan's chief US economist put it plainly, that the Fed risks its credibility if it doesn't back up its rhetoric with action. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is now navigating this in direct tension with President Trump, who's been pushing publicly for lower rates. That's an unusual dynamic to explain to clients: a central bank that may hike specifically because inflation is proving stickier than politically convenient.

Equity markets are reacting to two things at once, the oil shock and a sudden wave of caution out of the artificial intelligence industry. Anthropic's CEO published an open letter over the weekend calling for a slowdown in AI development and pledged to do so unilaterally, and OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and others echoed the call. That's rattled the exact stocks that have carried this market's momentum. SoftBank shares dropped double digits in Tokyo, memory chip makers in Korea and Japan fell hard, and Nvidia was down in US premarket trading this morning. Nasdaq futures are leading losses. Here in Canada, TSX futures are following that lower ahead of the inflation print, even though Friday's session was actually positive, up about half a percent, led by names like Boyd Group and Celestica. Tell clients this is a valuation and momentum story on top of a supply shock story, and that the two are reinforcing each other right now rather than offsetting.

On currency, the loonie is weaker again today. The Canadian dollar weakened against its U.S. counterpart, trading in a range of 71.92 to 72.13 US cents, down about 0.17 per cent over the past month. A stronger US dollar index and rising rate expectations south of the border are the main drag. For anyone with US dollar exposure or upcoming cross-border spending, this is worth a quick mention.

Now the domestic story that's actually dominating Bay Street this week, even more than rates: the Canada Investment Summit running today and tomorrow in Toronto. Prime Minister Carney is pitching the country to roughly two dozen sources' worth of global capital, with a goal of one trillion dollars in investment over five years. More than 160 projects are on the table, including a proposed high speed rail link between Edmonton and Calgary and a Port of Churchill expansion, which matters to anyone in this room with Manitoba exposure, and Manitoba Hydro is worth watching if energy infrastructure spending flows this way. TD committed 150 billion dollars and Scotiabank committed 100 billion dollars this morning to fund Canadian companies in critical sectors, and Scotiabank has also brought on former US ambassador Kirsten Hillman to advise its new Scotia Growth Institute, which is on your watch list too. On trade, Trump told reporters this weekend a Canada-US deal could come fairly soon, and Carney has echoed that he doesn't expect further retaliation from either side. That's a meaningfully more constructive tone than we've had in months.

One more thread worth a sentence with clients: Canada is quietly exploring deeper ties with the European Union, possibly even some kind of associate status, as a hedge against overreliance on Washington. And on housing, the Globe's own reporting this morning flags that the market should brace for more strain heading into 2027, tied to affordability and borrowing costs that aren't falling as fast as some homeowners had hoped. Worth keeping on your radar for renewal conversations this fall.
talkingPoints: Oil just spiked on a Saudi pipeline shutdown, and that's the wildcard for both inflation and your energy holdings this week.
Today's Canadian inflation number is expected to hold near 3 per cent, with the Bank of Canada watching whether energy costs bleed into everything else.
The Bank of Canada's rate decision is on the watch list, next one October 28th, and a hike in early 2027 is now a real possibility, not a hold forever story.
The Fed decides Wednesday and markets are now betting on a hike, not a cut, which is an awkward message for anyone expecting lower borrowing costs soon.
Carney's trillion dollar investment summit in Toronto, plus TD and Scotiabank's big financing commitments, is the most constructive Canadian growth story we've had in a while.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: AI Giants Call for Slowdown as Markets Wobble
blocks.script:
Good evening. Here is your roundup of the day's top business and world news.

The biggest story tonight comes from Silicon Valley, where the leaders of the world's largest AI companies are suddenly talking about hitting the brakes. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an open letter over the weekend calling for a global slowdown in AI development, according to Bloomberg's Markets Daily newsletter. Amodei warned that AI has been advancing drastically faster this summer, driven by the technology's growing ability to build its own successors, and said this risks AI outrunning humanity's ability to understand and control it.

Amodei also committed Anthropic to giving outside evaluators permanent, employee-level access to its systems so they can check safety measures and flag problems.

He wasn't alone. OpenAI's Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis, and Elon Musk all backed the call for a slower pace, Bloomberg reports. Altman said OpenAI would offer similar access to independent evaluators, and confirmed he's pushing the company's planned stock market listing back to at least 2027, calling this an ill-advised moment to go public.

Not everyone is convinced this is really about safety. White House AI chief David Sacks described the industry's sudden caution as a bid for regulatory capture, according to The Peak newsletter. President Trump himself has downplayed the warnings, according to the BBC, suggesting that concerns are being raised by, in his words, negative forces worried about things that won't happen, and pointing to competition with China as a reason to keep pushing forward.

Meanwhile, a former Anthropic researcher told the BBC that AI safety staff are genuinely frightened for humanity's future, even as the BBC also reports that some in Silicon Valley are treating the dramatic warnings with skepticism. In Britain, MPs and members of the House of Lords are calling for new legislation to address AI's threat to human rights, arguing existing law isn't equipped to handle it. And former President Obama has urged Democrats to develop a clear plan on AI safeguards, calling it a central issue the party needs to address.

Markets felt the jitters immediately. Bloomberg's Markets Daily reports that AI bellwether stocks took a hit, with SoftBank shares sliding eleven percent in Tokyo. Chipmakers were hammered too, with South Korea's SK Hynix and Samsung both down sharply, and Europe's ASML falling more than four percent. In the United States, Nvidia and memory chip makers were lower in premarket trading. On the flip side, software companies seen as less exposed to an AI slowdown, including Adobe, Salesforce, and Crowdstrike, all gained ground.

Adding to market anxiety, oil prices jumped after Saudi Arabia was forced to close a major crude pipeline following drone attacks, according to Bloomberg. Traders say as much as four percent of global oil supply could be at risk, on top of ongoing disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, where a planned meeting between Iran and Gulf nations on the shipping lane has reportedly been postponed. Separately, Yemen's Houthi rebels have seized more islands in the southern Red Sea, according to the Globe and Mail, tightening their grip on a major maritime route and prompting Somali shippers to look for alternative paths.

Turning to Canada, Prime Minister Mark Carney is kicking off his Canada Investment Summit in Toronto this week, seeking roughly one trillion dollars in commitments from major global investors, according to CBC. More than 167 projects are reportedly on the table. Canadian banks are already lining up behind the effort. The Globe and Mail reports TD has committed 150 billion dollars to fund Canadian companies in critical sectors over five years, while Scotiabank has pledged more than 100 billion dollars for similar expansion, tapping former U.S. ambassador Kirsten Hillman to help lead the push. Protests are also planned around the summit, with organizers objecting to putting the country's economic future in the hands of corporate executives, the Globe and Mail reports.

On trade, President Trump told reporters over the weekend that a deal between the U.S. and Canada could be coming fairly soon, downplaying talk of the U.S. walking away from the CUSMA agreement, according to The Peak. Carney struck a similarly optimistic note last week, saying he doesn't expect further tariff retaliation from either side. Separately, CBC reports Canadian exports to China rose about 30 percent in the first half of 2026, even as imports from China declined, according to data from the Canada-China Business Council and the University of Alberta.

In Europe, exit polls show Sweden's centre-left bloc winning the country's parliamentary election, a result that bucks the rightward trend seen elsewhere on the continent, Reuters reports via The Peak. The result was described as an unexpectedly poor showing for the right-wing Sweden Democrats.

And in Britain, Prime Minister Burnham is urging a culture shift in how the UK does business, saying risk-takers deserve government backing, even as his administration faces criticism for raising business costs, the BBC reports. Separately, property website Zoopla forecasts rents in the UK will accelerate, rising four to five percent a year by December.
talkingPoints: Major AI firms including Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google DeepMind are calling for a slower pace of development, citing loss-of-control risks, while critics call it regulatory capture.
Global markets wobbled on the AI slowdown talk and on oil price spikes following attacks on Saudi pipeline infrastructure and ongoing Red Sea and Hormuz disruptions.
Canada's Carney is seeking roughly a trillion dollars in investment commitments at a Toronto summit this week, backed by major bank pledges, amid protests and trade talks with Washington.

blocks.label: Practice: Tax, Regulatory & Industry
blocks.title: Registered Plans, CIRO Breach, and Rate Watch
blocks.script:
Start with the one that affects how you talk to every client this week. The Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, that's CIRO, the national self-regulator for investment and mutual fund dealers, is still working through its cybersecurity incident. CIRO has confirmed the breach hit registration data, not the National Registration Database itself, and the organization began sending letters to affected individuals beginning September 9. That's this week. If you get calls from clients who received one of those letters, the message is simple: their trading system wasn't touched, this is registration information CIRO holds, and CIRO has said it's conducting a renewed review of its data retention policies. Worth raising proactively with anyone who's had a CIRO-registered advisor over the years, even ones they've since left.

Layer onto that a second CIRO story that's more about your own file hygiene. New proficiency rules took effect January 1 this year, meaning newly approved registered representatives need a relevant diploma or degree, or four years of relevant experience, before they get approved. And on the documentation side, CIRO hearing panels have been sanctioning firms over what is or isn't in the client file. National Bank Financial accepted a settlement this past March over a failure to properly supervise note-taking and suitability documentation on one representative's book. CIRO's also running a Rule Consolidation Project that will reshape know-your-client and suitability documentation once finalized. Translation for your practice: your meeting notes need to show the reasoning, not just the recommendation.

Now the numbers you'll actually use in review meetings this fall. The 2026 Registered Retirement Savings Plan dollar limit is $33,810, up from $32,490 in 2025. Remember that's capped at 18 percent of prior year earned income, so a client earning $150,000 gets roughly $27,000 in new room, not the full dollar limit. Tax-Free Savings Account room added another $7,000 on January 1, same as the past two years, which puts cumulative room at $109,000 for anyone eligible since 2009 who's never contributed. First Home Savings Account holders get $8,000 of new room a year toward a $40,000 lifetime cap, and withdrawals for a qualifying first home stay tax-free. Registered Education Savings Plan lifetime contribution room per beneficiary is $50,000. For your incorporated business owners and physicians, this is the moment to revisit the salary versus dividend decision before year-end bonus declarations, since RRSP room only builds off salaried, T4 income, not dividends.

On the macro side, Statistics Canada put out August inflation this morning, and the Street was looking for headline Consumer Price Index growth to hold around 3 percent, unchanged from July, per Investment Executive and the Globe and Mail. Gasoline was still running about 23 percent above year-ago levels even after easing in August, RBC economist Nathan Janzen noted. Core measures, which strip out food and energy, are sitting closer to 2 percent, and that's what the Bank of Canada actually watches. The Globe reports another hold looks likely at the Bank's October 28 decision, though Governor Tiff Macklem has flagged he'd consider hiking if energy costs spill into broader prices. That decision stays on your watch list heading into the fourth quarter.

On the industry side, both TD and Scotiabank made headlines today with big Canadian financing commitments tied to the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto. TD is putting $150 billion toward Canadian companies in critical sectors over five years, and Scotiabank, parent of Scotia Wealth Management, is committing $100 billion. That's on your watch list given the Scotia Wealth Management connection, and it signals both banks leaning harder into domestic corporate lending as Ottawa tries to court foreign capital. Separately, CIBC earmarked $2 billion for small and medium-sized defence firms, part of the same push to scale domestic manufacturing capacity.

On product and fee trends, Advisor.ca flags rising client interest in annuities, driven by higher interest rates making guaranteed income products more attractive again. Worth raising with any client approaching retirement or already in a life transition, since a rate environment like this one is exactly when annuities start pricing more competitively against a pure drawdown strategy. Investment Executive's product roundup also shows Vanguard launching an actively managed fixed-income exchange-traded fund, alongside new offerings from Manulife, Capstone, Hamilton ETFs, Corton Capital and Smead Canada. Active strategies keep pushing into ETF wrappers, and that's worth a line in any fee conversation this month.

Two more for your file. A former tech executive resolved a Securities and Exchange Commission insider trading case in the U.S. after trading ahead of negative earnings news, a reminder to keep pre-clearance conversations current with any client who sits on a board or has material non-public information exposure. And closer to home, the Globe reports a second TD investor has alleged fraudulent trades in an obscure Chinese stock, following an earlier Alberta case with what sounds like an identical pattern. Given the CIRO breach news, this is a good week to walk clients through how to spot unauthorized account activity.

Last one, and it touches your professional client base directly. The Globe reports on Canadian students going abroad for medical school because of competitive domestic admissions, often at substantially higher cost. If you advise young physicians, that debt load now shows up years before incorporation and passive income planning even start, so factor it into any new physician's five-year plan before you talk about setting up a professional corporation.
talkingPoints: The CIRO breach letters going out this week are about registration data, not trading access, so reassure before you explain.

Rising rates are pulling annuities back into retirement income conversations, worth a mention with anyone near retirement.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Hydro Tariffs, Bank of Canada Hold, Daycare Scandal
blocks.script:
The story with the biggest dollar signs for your clients today is Manitoba Hydro, and it is two stories rolled into one. The Canada-U.S. trade war has complicated Manitoba Hydro's plan to buy gas turbines for its $3-billion Brandon generating station expansion from a manufacturer based in Massachusetts. Layer onto that the fact that six weeks of public hearings into Manitoba Hydro's generating plans came to an end with more criticism of the Crown corporation's proposed natural gas expansion in Brandon. If you have clients with Hydro bonds, Hydro pension exposure, or just a mortgage tied to provincial rate assumptions, this is worth watching. A three billion dollar capital project running into tariff friction on its main equipment supplier is the kind of thing that shows up later as a rate application.

Speaking of rates, the Bank of Canada is on your watch list, and it held its target for the overnight rate at 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20%, on September second. That makes a seventh consecutive hold. The Bank flagged the war in the Middle East and new US tariffs as live risks to inflation, language it used to justify staying put rather than cutting further. The next scheduled date for announcing the overnight rate target is October 28, 2026. So if a client asks why nothing moved, tell them that is your next real decision point.

Closer to home, CBC Manitoba has a story that will come up at any board table this week: a five and a half million dollar daycare, built two years ago with provincial funds in the East St. Paul area, is now sitting vacant, plundered by scavengers, and damaged by flooding. That is public money, spent on a facility meant to add child care spaces in a province that has spent years talking up its child care expansion, and it is now a boarded up shell. Expect questions about how that gets audited and who signed off on it.

On the trade file, CBC reports Manitoba sports organizations and retailers are pushing governments on both sides of the border to suspend tariffs on sports equipment, warning that higher prices could reduce participation in youth and recreational sports. For retail clients or anyone with exposure to sporting goods distribution in this province, that is a small but real margin squeeze story, and it lines up with the broader tariff drag the Bank of Canada itself is watching.

Manitoba's other big engine, agriculture, got a research update from CBC Manitoba out of Brandon, where scientists at Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada are racing to breed crops that can handle heat and drought, work aimed squarely at protecting yields on the hundreds of acres surrounding the city. If you have farm clients in the Westman region, or bank shares tied to grain handling, that research pipeline is part of what protects revenue when the growing season turns hostile.

On the Blue Bombers, also on your watch list, Winnipeg beat Saskatchewan nineteen to six at the Banjo Bowl on Saturday at Princess Auto Stadium. Safety Redha Kramdi, back from a broken hand, played what CBC called a huge role in the win. Good dinner table material this week if you have Bomber season ticket holders as clients.

Finally, three community stories worth knowing even if they are not balance sheet items. Steinbach held its Pride event this weekend after last year's was postponed over safety threats, and CBC reports marchers said they were not going to hide. About one hundred people gathered at The Forks for the third annual Fentanyl Awareness walk. And the family of Tanya Nepinak marked fifteen years since she went missing in Winnipeg's West End, a reminder that cases like hers still shape how this city talks about policing priorities.

That is Manitoba and Winnipeg for today.

blocks.label: Canadian Politics
blocks.title: Carney's Toronto Pitch, Hydro's Trade War Headache
blocks.script:
Prime Minister Mark Carney spent Sunday night in Toronto trying to turn a headline number into real deals. The Canada Investment Summit opened at the Royal Ontario Museum, and the room included premiers, cabinet ministers and executives from BlackRock, RBC, Scotiabank and CPP Investments. Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew was on the guest list alongside the other provincial leaders. Carney told the crowd that investors managing over 120 trillion dollars in assets are looking at Canada differently now, and that there's a new consensus from Iqaluit to Victoria that the country is taking control of its future. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says she expects the summit, running through Tuesday at the Four Seasons, to produce actual deal announcements, not just talk. Officials have circulated a list of more than 160 projects open for investment, and two are worth flagging for a Manitoba audience: a proposed 57 billion dollar expansion at the Port of Churchill, and a 10.9 billion dollar high speed rail link between Edmonton and Calgary. On the financing side, TD committed 150 billion dollars and Scotiabank committed 100 billion dollars to fund Canadian companies over the next five years. Scotia Wealth Management's parent bank making that kind of commitment is on the watch list worth noting for clients who ask where the big banks are putting capital.

Statistics Canada put out August inflation numbers this morning. The Street expected headline CPI to hold at 3 percent year over year, unchanged from July, with gasoline still running about 23 percent above last year despite easing slightly last month. Grocery inflation has outpaced the overall rate for roughly a year and a half, which keeps squeezing lower income households hardest. Core measures, which strip out food and energy, are running closer to 2 percent, and that's what the Bank of Canada watches most closely. The Bank of Canada rate decision is on the watch list: another hold is expected October 28, though Governor Tiff Macklem has said the bank would consider raising rates if energy costs spill into broader prices. Most economists don't see a hike this year, but the odds of one in early 2027 are rising.

Closer to home, Manitoba Hydro is on the watch list and had a rough couple of weeks. Six weeks of public hearings into the utility's generating plans wrapped up with continued criticism of its proposal to expand natural gas burning at its Brandon station. Separately, the Canada-US trade war has complicated Manitoba Hydro's plan to buy gas turbines for that same three billion dollar Brandon expansion from a Massachusetts manufacturer. That's a direct, local example of how tariff friction is showing up in provincial infrastructure planning, not just in the news out of Ottawa.

On the diplomatic front, Carney is set to address the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday. Ottawa wants deeper trade, investment, security and labour ties with the European Union, but a senior government official says not at the expense of Canadian sovereignty. The Wall Street Journal reported Carney had floated the idea of Canada as an associate member of the EU, though a Canadian government source pushed back, saying it was the EU, not Carney, that raised the idea, and that any formal arrangement is premature. Carney also meets his British counterpart this week for the first time, and travels to Saint-Pierre and Miquelon next week to meet French President Emmanuel Macron on energy and defence.

None of this happens separate from the tariff fight with Washington. Canada and the US remain stuck in their trade war positions, and some Democratic politicians in Washington argue a strong showing for their party in the November midterms would shift Trump's approach to Canada. That's a bet, not a certainty, and it's one more reason the investment summit's emphasis on non-US capital, from European and Gulf investors, matters for how exposed Canadian portfolios are to a single trading partner.
talkingPoints: The Canada Investment Summit in Toronto is pitching over 160 projects, including a Churchill port expansion relevant to Manitoba trade routes.

blocks.label: Climate Policy & Nonprofit Governance
blocks.title: Manitoba Gas Fight, Ottawa's Investment Pitch, United Way's Record Year
blocks.script:
The biggest energy story out of Manitoba this week wrapped up last Wednesday. Six weeks of public hearings into Manitoba Hydro's generating plan closed with more pushback on the utility's proposal to burn more natural gas, CBC News reports. Six weeks of public hearings into Manitoba Hydro's generating plans came to an end with more criticism of the Crown corporation's proposed natural gas expansion in Brandon, and the Public Utilities Board spent late July to early September scrutinizing the integrated resource plan. That plan calls for 1,760 more megawatts of electricity, more than a quarter of Hydro's existing generating capacity, over the next decade. It leans on 600 megawatts of new Indigenous majority owned wind power, but also roughly 750 megawatts of new gas turbines, and several groups told the board in closing arguments that Hydro hadn't made its case for the gas piece.

That matters for anyone with Manitoba Hydro exposure or rate sensitivity, because the bill side is already locked in. The Public Utilities Board finalized a 4 per cent general rate increase effective January 1, 2026, with further increases of 3.5 per cent in 2027 and 3 per cent in 2028, framed as front-loading revenue to respond to drought impacts on hydroelectric generation. Manitoba Hydro is on the watch list this week for that reason: rates are settled through 2028, but the gas-versus-wind fight over how the utility grows past that point is still live and unresolved.

Zoom out to the national picture. Prime Minister Mark Carney opened his first Investment Summit in Toronto on Monday, pitching global investors on Canada, according to Canada's National Observer. Clean Energy Canada used the moment to make its own point. The group's program manager said the deal book released last week showcases Canada's potential to become a clean energy superpower while highlighting a gap between ambition and the money actually moving. Worth raising with clients who hold Canadian infrastructure or utility names: the ambition is loud right now, the capital commitments are still catching up.

Meanwhile in Alberta, Premier Danielle Smith said this weekend it's unlikely her government will launch a new Crown corporation to build gas pipelines, after a report on the idea leaked, per Canada's National Observer. So in one week you've got Manitoba's utility leaning into gas at the generation level, Alberta backing away from a state-run gas pipeline vehicle, and Ottawa trying to sell the country as a clean electricity destination, all pulling in slightly different directions.

On the charitable side, United Way Winnipeg closed its 2025 campaign with a record result. The organization says Winnipeggers raised a record-breaking $23.3 million for United Way Winnipeg's 2025 campaign, and it has named Anne Mahon, Chancellor Emeritus of the University of Manitoba, and Paul Mahon, former President and CEO of Canada Life, as co-chairs of the 2026 campaign. United Way Winnipeg is on the watch list this week for that reason.

For governance conversations with nonprofit board clients, here's a useful benchmark: United Way Winnipeg is accredited by Imagine Canada's Standards Program, a set of 73 standards that ensure effective, accountable, and ethical practices in nonprofit governance and management. That's a concrete, third-party standard you can point clients toward when they're vetting a charity's board practices before a major gift or a board seat, rather than relying on a glossy annual report alone.
talkingPoints: Manitoba Hydro's gas expansion plan just cleared six weeks of hostile hearings, worth flagging for utility-exposed holdings.
Hydro rates are locked through 2028 at 4, 3.5, and 3 percent, so build that into retiree cash flow planning now.
Ottawa's investment summit is heavy on clean energy talk, but Clean Energy Canada says the capital isn't matching the ambition yet.
Alberta just stepped back from a state-run gas pipeline company, a sign provinces are still feeling out the right structure.
United Way Winnipeg's $23.3 million record campaign and its Imagine Canada accreditation are a solid governance reference point for nonprofit clients.

blocks.label: AI & Technology
blocks.title: Anthropic's Slowdown Call Meets Wall Street Money
blocks.script:
The biggest story this week is Dario Amodei's essay calling for the industry to pace the frontier. The Anthropic chief executive published a thirty eight hundred word piece on Saturday arguing that development of the most advanced AI systems needs to slow down to avoid losing control of them. What makes this notable is who signed on: OpenAI's Sam Altman and Elon Musk's SpaceXAI both endorsed it. Bloomberg reports that Anthropic and OpenAI will have to weigh this against forces in the tech industry, financial markets, and the Trump administration that are likely to resist any real slowdown, especially with both companies eyeing potentially record setting initial public offerings that depend on continued frontier breakthroughs. Amodei insists pacing doesn't mean less spending or growth, but that's a hard sell to investors betting on hundreds of billions in capital expenditure.

Worth knowing for client conversations: President Trump publicly downplayed these risk warnings, per the BBC, framing them as negative forces raising concerns about things that won't happen, and tying it to competition with China. On the other side, Barack Obama told Democrats this week, according to TechCrunch, that AI needs to become a central agenda item with a clear plan on economic impact and safety. So you've got a real partisan split forming on how this gets regulated, which matters if you're advising anyone with exposure to AI infrastructure names.

There's also a useful counter frame here. Researchers Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor argue AI should be treated as a normal technology, not an incomprehensible superintelligence in waiting, and that view is gaining traction as a check on the doom messaging. BetaKit's newsletter this week flagged the AI bubble red flags directly: circular financing arrangements between chip makers, cloud providers, and model companies, plus concerns about rogue agentic tools operating with too little oversight. That's the kind of structural risk worth mentioning if a client asks why you're not chasing every AI headline into their portfolio.

On the Canadian side, BetaKit also reports Canada and Ukraine have struck a binational deal tapping Canadian drone companies, with firms from New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, and Saskatchewan receiving contracts. That's a real, if narrow, data point on where Canadian tech dollars and government procurement are actually flowing right now, defence and dual use tech rather than pure consumer AI.

Now the part that touches your clients directly. The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre's 2025 figures show Canadians lost a record seven hundred four million dollars to fraud last year, up from six hundred forty five million in 2024, with investment fraud alone accounting for three hundred fifty one million of that. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security has separately warned that AI is shrinking the time defenders have to respond to attacks, from days down to hours, because generative tools let scammers write convincing phishing emails and voice clones at scale. If you haven't already, this is the week to remind clients that a phone call sounding exactly like a family member asking for a wire transfer is not proof of anything.

One item for the watch list: the Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at two and a quarter percent at its September second decision, the seventh straight hold, citing energy prices tied to the Middle East conflict and fresh trade tension with Washington. The next decision is October twenty eighth, and Governor Tiff Macklem's language suggests no clear signal either way until then.

Net for you: the AI story right now isn't about a new model release, it's about who controls the pace of the next one, and whether regulation lands before or after the capital keeps flowing.
talkingPoints: Anthropic's own chief executive is now the one calling for a slowdown, and Musk and Altman backed him.
Trump and Obama are on opposite sides of how hard to regulate AI, which will shape the policy risk in AI-heavy portfolios.
Canadian fraud losses hit a record seven hundred four million dollars last year, with investment scams the single largest category.
Ottawa's cyber centre says AI is cutting response time for defenders from days to hours, so verify any urgent money request by a second channel.
The Bank of Canada held rates again on September second, seventh straight hold, next decision October twenty eighth.

blocks.label: Health & Fitness
blocks.title: Strength Training Longevity Data, Creatine, and RSV Gaps
blocks.script:
The biggest health story this week comes from Harvard's T.H. Chan School of Public Health, published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine. The study looked at three decades' worth of data from nearly 150,000 adults participating in three long-running studies, the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study, the Nurses' Health Study, and the Nurses' Health Study II. Roughly 90-120 minutes of strength training per week was linked with a 13% reduced risk of premature death, according to the study. Adults who averaged that range of weekly resistance training had a 13% lower risk of early death from any cause, a 19% lower risk from heart disease specifically. Adding aerobic exercise to the weekly mix increased the longevity benefit further. This is a long-running observational study, not a randomized trial, so it shows association, not proof of cause. But the sample size and three decades of tracking make it one of the stronger pieces of evidence yet that lifting does real work for longevity, not just muscle. The takeaway for someone who already lifts twice a week is that you're already in the zone where the data show the biggest return. No need to chase more volume for longevity's sake.

On the supplement side, Examine.com published a summary this year of a meta-analysis of 61 randomized controlled trials in 1,457 participants, finding that creatine combined with resistance training increased fat-free mass equally well in both trained and untrained lifters. So if you've been putting off creatine because you thought it was only for advanced lifters, the evidence doesn't back that up.

For the mobility side of training, Outside magazine published five yoga-inspired exercises for feet, ankles, and calves, aimed at people who hike or run outdoors. The logic holds in the gym too: weak ankle stability shows up as wobble under a loaded squat or lunge, and a few minutes of targeted foot and ankle work before a session is cheap insurance against rolled ankles and shifted form.

On the Canadian health system side, CBC reports that Nova Scotia's RSV, that's respiratory syncytial virus, vaccination program only covers three specific groups for free, leaving some seniors and immunocompromised people to pay out of pocket, a few hundred dollars per dose. It's a reminder that provincial vaccine coverage varies a lot across the country, worth checking directly with Manitoba Health if clients ask about their own eligibility this fall.
talkingPoints: Ninety to 120 minutes of strength training a week is linked to a 13% lower risk of early death, per a 30 year Harvard study.
Two lifting sessions a week already puts you in the sweet spot for the longevity benefit.
Creatine works just as well for beginners as for experienced lifters, per a new 61 trial meta-analysis.
A few minutes of ankle and foot mobility work protects your squat and lunge form.
Nova Scotia's free RSV vaccine program excludes some seniors, a reminder provincial health coverage varies across Canada.

blocks.label: Parenting
blocks.title: Canada Child Benefit Rises, Screen Time Guidance Holds Firm
blocks.script:
The biggest line for parents this year is a bank account, not a diagnosis. The Canada Child Benefit reset its payments in July, and Ottawa confirmed the new maximums this summer: up to eight thousand one hundred fifty seven dollars a year for a child under six, and up to six thousand eight hundred eighty three dollars for a child six to seventeen. That is an increase of up to $160 per child under age 6 and up to $135 per child aged 6 to 17 compared to the previous year. A family with one child aged 5 and one aged 9, with adjusted family net income of $65,000, will receive approximately $11,430 in 2026 to 27, nearly $400 more than the year before. The benefit has been indexed to inflation every year since 2018, so this is predictable, not a one off top up. For clients, that is real monthly cash flow worth revisiting, especially the question of whether some of it should flow straight into a Registered Education Savings Plan, or RESP, to capture the matching Canada Education Savings Grant.

On the paediatric side, guidance has not shifted this month. Canadian guidelines recommend no screen time for children under two, and for children two to five, routine or sedentary screen time limited to one hour or less per day. Canadian Paediatric Society principles still centre on minimizing, mitigating, mindfully using, and modelling healthy screen use rather than a strict stopwatch.

Separately, the Globe and Mail has a piece today on breakfast and school focus, citing evidence that a nutritious morning meal helps kids think and learn better in the classroom. Small, practical, consistent with what paediatric nutrition guidance has said for years, and worth passing along to clients juggling early drop offs.

That extra cash flow is a good prompt to revisit RESP contributions and the grant match.

blocks.label: Sports
blocks.title: Bombers Survive, Jets Camp Looms, Hellebuyck Watch
blocks.script:
The Winnipeg Blue Bombers beat the Saskatchewan Roughriders 19 to 6 in the Banjo Bowl on Saturday at Princess Auto Stadium. That puts them at 7 and 6, back in the thick of the West Division playoff race, per the Globe and Mail. The real story out of that game is quarterback Zach Collaros. He left in the third quarter with an undisclosed upper body injury after taking a beating, four of Saskatchewan's five sacks landed on him, and he finished 13 for 19 for 175 yards, a touchdown and two interceptions before backup Dru Brown closed it out, 4 for 5 for 46 yards, per CBC. Safety Redha Kramdi, back from a six game stretch on the injured list with a broken hand, forced a fumble and sealed the win with a fourth quarter interception. The Bombers are on their bye this week and return September 25th hosting the Toronto Argonauts. Watch for a Collaros update before then. Both the Bombers and the Jets are on your watch list, so this is a two team morning.

On the Jets, training camp opens Thursday at Hockey For All Centre. Preseason starts September 19th in Edmonton against the Oilers, then two home dates at Canada Life Centre, Colorado on the 21st and the Oilers again on the 22nd. The regular season is tentatively pegged for September 29th at home. The story hanging over camp is goaltender Connor Hellebuyck. He has requested a trade and has stayed off the ice at informal skates in Winnipeg. Captain Adam Lowry says the speculation is not worth the team's time, and Mark Scheifele says he still believes in this group coming off a career year of his own. If it is not resolved before the opener, expect it to follow the team on the road, and expect it to come up at every dinner table in the city.

Elsewhere in the NHL, new Maple Leafs general manager Chayka told the Globe and Mail he understands the weight of running the team he cheered for as a kid, after Toronto missed the playoffs last season for the first time since 2016. In Montreal, the Canadiens signed forward Zachary Bolduc to a four year extension, per CBC.

In the NFL, Sunday delivered the highest scoring season opener in league history as the Bears beat the Panthers, per the Globe and Mail. Kirk Cousins threw three touchdowns and joined the 300 touchdown club as the Raiders beat the Dolphins 27 to 13. Detroit escaped New Orleans in overtime, 31 to 30, with Jahmyr Gibbs putting up a career high 29 carries for 156 yards and two touchdowns. Buffalo got a late touchdown from Josh Allen to Joshua Palmer to beat Houston, their first win there since 2006. On the injury side, the reigning NFL Defensive Player of the Year, Myles Garrett, needs knee surgery and is headed to injured reserve, out at least four games, per The Athletic.

In the NBA, Clippers owner Steve Ballmer said this weekend his team will accept the league's penalties for circumventing the salary cap to funnel money to Kawhi Leonard. He called it sincere regrets in a statement, per The Athletic.

Tonight closes out week one of the NFL with Monday Night Football. The CFL is quiet with the Bombers on their bye, and the NBA stays in the off season while Jets camp opens in three days.
